messages.subject: Re: Computational Efficiency Discrepancy
messages.subject_clean: Computational Efficiency Discrepancy
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ben

If the issue is that adaptive Metropolis-Hastings efficiency is being decreased due to bounds on the parameter space, then you may like to try the nimbleNoBounds <https://cran.r-project.org/package=nimbleNoBounds> package. I tried this and added code to your scripts to quantify efficiency (attached), and noticed that the efficiency for sampling tau can be increased (very) roughly by 3 times, although the efficiency gain for sampling eps on a transformed scale is less convincing. However, the key bottle-neck with sampling your model is the extremely large auto-correlation in the delta. The functions effectiveSize and acfplot from the coda library can provide helpful diagnostics in your quest for better mixing.

Cheers
David

On Friday, 29 July 2022 at 17:47:43 UTC+2 Ben Lee wrote:
> Hi Perry,
>
> As always, thank you and the rest of the nimble team for the quick and detailed response. This makes absolute sense that we are rejecting too many proposals because we use uniform priors for eps. In the next stage, we will try a scaling/translation such as logit(eps) and use the multivariate normal proposal. We really appreciate your attention to this matter.
>
> best,
> Ben
>
> On Friday, July 29, 2022 at 11:05:03 AM UTC-4 pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Remy,
> >
> > Thanks for the question and very clear reproducible code.  It was puzzling but I think I know what is going on.
> >
> > First I checked on time spent in each sampler, using
> > cmcmcRmodel$run(niter, time = TRUE)
> > cmcmcRmodel$samplerTimes
> >
> > The second sampler accounts for essentially all of the difference in computing time (about 8 seconds difference on my machine out of 25 or 34 seconds in the two cases, so quite noticeable).
> > From
> > confRModel$printSamplers()
> > we see that the second sampler is for eps.  This will have the expensive computations of M as a dependency.
> >
> > Yet the computations of the pieces of M itself are not counter-intuitive in terms of computational cost.
> > system.time(for(i in 1:100) cRmodel$calculate("M")) # Loop 100 times for some averaging of costs
> > # This is nearly the same in the two cases but slightly *faster* when you've used 2 sub-matrices instead of 10.  That makes sense and is opposite to the weird MCMC result.  Also note that there will be some overhead in R when nimble evaluates cRmodel$calculate("M").  It will be in R that it determines what nodes need calculation, and sets up a loop for that, so that may account for some of the slowdown for 10.  But the difference is 2.1  seconds (case 10) vs 2.0 seconds (case 2) on my machine, so not of the magnitude in the MCMC issue.
> > So this suggests it is not raw computation time of the M pieces that is the issue.
> >
> > I think what is happening is that invalid proposals (outside support of the prior) in the block sampler are immediately rejected without wasting time computing dependencies, and this is much more likely to happen in the case of 10 elements for eps than 2 elements for eps.  To explain more, your eps[1:q] is a vector node, meaning it is (by default MCMC configuration) sampled as a vector using an adaptive random-walk Metropolis-Hastings  block sampler.  And the prior is your dUnifVector which makes it uniform from 1 to 3 in every element.  The RW-MH block sampler makes multivariate normal proposals, for which the scale and correlation are adapted over many iterations and might be quite poor (arbitrary) choices at the start.  Like many of our samplers, after it makes a proposal, it first checks the log probability of the prior.  If that is -Inf (meaning the proposal is in a region of 0 prior probability) it immediately rejects the proposal and that iteration of that sampler is done.  When this occurs the dependency computations are *not* done.  In your case, every time an invalid proposal is made, the cost of computing M (all of its pieces) is skipped because the proposal will be rejected regardless.  A block sampler in 10 dimensions with uniform prior is much more likely to have at least one element fall outside of the valid range (1 to 3) and thus have the whole vector proposal be immediately rejected.  Also I noticed from the posterior that elements of eps can spend a lot of time (iterations) up against a boundary value, making it likely that a proposal will be on the invalid side of that boundary.  In other words, the case of 10 goes faster because it is more often making waster proposals for eps[1:10] that are rejected without incurring the cost of computing M (and then W, lambda and Z)
> >
> > I'm not sure of the full context here, but some ideas are: you could set up eps as scalar nodes and they will be sampled one by one; and/or you could set up eps on a different scale, like logit(eps), so they do not have the boundaries from the uniform.  Or you may have just wanted to make sense of what nimble is doing.
> >
> > The cost of the actual multivariate normal draw and adaptation inside the RW-MH block sampler in this case is very small compared to the model computations.
> >
> > I hope that is clear!
> >
> > Perry
> >
> > On Thu, Jul 28, 2022 at 10:39 PM Remy MacDonald <remyn...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I have encountered a counter-intuitive discrepancy in the computational cost between two MCMC algorithms and was hoping you would have insight into why this could be occurring,
> > >
> > > In MCMC2.R (which sources nimbleToy2.R) the nimble function involves splitting X into two sub-matrices and evaluating a function of each sub-matrix. On the other hand, with MCMC10.R, the nimble function involves splitting X into ten sub-matrices. I'm finding that the latter is more computationally efficient even though there are more parameters which need to be estimated (eps1,...,eps10 verses eps1,eps2). In fact, if we increase the number of sub matrices and corresponding values of epsilon, the efficiency only improves.
> > >
> > > Please let me know if my question is unclear and I will try to clarify. Thank you so much!
> > >

messages.subject: Re: Indexing: non-conformable arguments
messages.subject_clean: Indexing: non-conformable arguments
messages.body_plain:
Zhihua, thanks for your email and your patience.

I took a quick look, and this is a subtle case indeed, with the dependency paths of your deterministic nodes in combination with the matrix multiplications, this enters into an obscure part of the conjugacy checking, which here gives an infinite recursion - the check repeatedly creats its own internal "structure expression" object to represent your calculations, then re-processes it over, and over, again.  Sorry, this bug is my fault.

I'll be working on a patch for our next release.  In the meantime, you can work around it easily by disabling the conjugacy checking:

longconf <- configureMCMC(longpro, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)

Let us know if this works for you.  And like I said, we'll get this fixed in a future release.

Cheers,
Daniel

> Hi Perry,
>
> Thank you for your answer and suggestion. I have modify the code and now the model can successfully be built and compiled. Thank you for your help.
> However, when I run "configureMCMC", errors show up as "Error in value[[3L]](cond) : node stack overflow
> Error during wrapup: node stack overflow
> Error: no more error handlers available (recursive errors?); invoking 'abort' restart"
> I don't know why this happens. Could you help me figure this out? The new version of my code is attached. Thank you so much!
> Best,
> Zhihua
>
> 在2022年7月29日星期五 UTC+8 21:58:21<pdevalpine> 写道：
> > Hi Zhu,
> > It looks like this error is coming from pure R (i.e. nimble uncompiled) calculation of your model.
> > It is happening when m[i] is 1.  In that case, (1+msum[i-1]):msum[i] is 1:1, or simply 1.  Then your quadratic form,
> >  E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6] %*% Sigma[1:6, 1:6] %*% t(E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6])
> > is not working correctly in R (or nimble).  Here is an example:
> > E <- 1:6 # E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6] returns a vector of length 6, so it is something of the same type as 1:6
> > Sigma <- diag(6)
> > E %*% Sigma %*% t(E) # error
> >
> > The problem is R dynamically evaluates the types of inputs to the %*% function.  When it sees a vector, it checks whether treating it as a one-row or one-column matrix will make it conformable. e.g. both of these work:
> > E %*% Sigma
> > Sigma %*% E
> >  But the default matrix for E is a one-column matrix, so t(E) is a one-row matrix, and this is non-conformable:  You are telling R which way you want it to handle E, and that way doesn't work.
> > Sigma %*% t(E)
> > Again, this error is occurring in R, but it is something you'll need to fix for nimble compilation to work as well.
> > There will also be an issue in nimble when you use extents like 1:m[i] that are simply 1:1.  So for both reasons, I'd suggest separating the cases where the extent is 1:1.  You could potentially pick those out separately and declare them in a for loop with scalar operations and a dnorm instead of dmnorm.
> >
> > I also noticed nimbleModel is giving you a warning (at the end of its output) about multiple declarations of mu_tau.  If that is indexed only by t, it should not be in a loop with i.  You can make a separate loop over t to declare the mu_tau nodes.
> >
> > I also noticed, in your R code for simulating inputs, the lines like
> > y[i,j] ~ rbinom(1, 1, 0.5)
> > are not doing anything.  In R code, you'll want "<-" instead of "~".
> >
> > HTH and good luck with it.
> > Perry
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Sally, Chris,

It seems this code attempts to implement the mixture of finite mixtures (MFM) approach of Miller and Harrison (https://jwmi.github.io/publications/MFM.pdf).

I believe that the dMCRP function should be defined on a vector of integers, i.e., we should have

dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
  run=function(x = integer(1),
...

Formally, the restaurant process is a mass function defined for a partition of integers {1, ..., n} e.g., x = (1, 1, 2, 2), for example, if there are two clusters.

In the paper, Miller and Harrison claim:
This is a direct adaptation of “Algorithm 3” for DPMs (MacEachern, 1994; Neal, 1992, 2000). The only differences are that in Algorithm 3, |c| + γ is replaced by |c|, and γVn(t + 1)/Vn(t) is replaced by α (the concentration parameter).

Is it possible to use the code in sampler_CRP to implement this change? I assume not since the normal CRP only has a single hyperparameter (alpha) and is a function of the number of clusters |c|. Here, we would have a second hyperparameter gamma that needs to be included in the sampling scheme.

> Hi Hanah,
>
> The specific issue is that you can't use arbitrary R code in defining your model (please see Section 5.2.5 of our manual). In particular, there's various R functions in these lines that won't work (rep, seq_along, as.numeric, tapply):
>
> g <- rep(seq_along(vec1), vec1)
> sumld<--as.numeric(tapply(lamda[vec2], g, sum))
>
> However, you can do this with some additional work. Your case is similar to another discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/b8G-1MtTm-c/m/smrwlsTUBAAJ> we had on the users group a while back. The basic idea is that you need to do the indexing as part of a nimbleFunction (because we don't support syntax like `sum(u[idx[1:4]])` directly in model code).
>
> Outside of your model code, write a nimbleFunction that does the mean calculation:
>
> mymean <- nimbleFunction(
>     run = function(lambda = double(1), nbrs = double(1), start = double(1), nb = double(1), i = double(0)) {
>         return(mean(lambda[nbrs[start[i]:(start[i]+nb[i]-1)]])
>         returnType(double(0))
>     }
> )
>
> Then in model code:
>
> u[i] <- mymean(lambda, nbrs, start, nb, i)
>
> You'd need to provide nbrs, idx and nb as constants. 'nbrs' should be vector containing the deltas, all strung together in a single vector. 'start' should be a vector indicating the first delta for each i.  Suppose that the delta_1 is {1,3} and delta_2 is {1,7,11}, and delta_3 is {2, 4} and so forth. Then 'start' is {1,3,6,...}.

I think that should get you going.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks, I haven't looked at this in detail, but I will respond now in hopes that some high-level feedback is helpful...

1) You would need `dMCRP` to use place of `dCRP`
2) You'd need a `sampler_MFM` to use in place of `sampler_CRP`. I believe that `sampler_MFM` would look similar to `sampler_CRP` but with the changes indicated in this email thread. I'm not sure how hard V_n(t) is to calculate...
3) There's no problem having an additional parameter (gamma). Hopefully one could assign some basic sampler to it (e.g., slice or RW) and it would mix ok. The sampling for gamma would happen separately from the sampling done by sampler_MFM .

Happy to continue to chat on this and help with guidance if someone tries to implement this.

-chris

> >
> > dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run=function(x = integer(1),
> > ...

> > Formally, the restaurant process is a mass function defined for a partition of integers {1, ..., n} e.g., x = (1, 1, 2, 2), for example, if there are two clusters.
> >
> > In the paper, Miller and Harrison claim:
> > This is a direct adaptation of “Algorithm 3” for DPMs (MacEachern, 1994; Neal, 1992, 2000). The only differences are that in Algorithm 3, |c| + γ is replaced by |c|, and γVn(t + 1)/Vn(t) is replaced by α (the concentration parameter).
> >
> > Is it possible to use the code in sampler_CRP to implement this change? I assume not since the normal CRP only has a single hyperparameter (alpha) and is a function of the number of clusters |c|. Here, we would have a second hyperparameter gamma that needs to be included in the sampling scheme.

Sorry, this bug is my fault.

> > > Hi Zhu,
> > > It looks like this error is coming from pure R (i.e. nimble uncompiled) calculation of your model.
> > > It is happening when m[i] is 1.  In that case, (1+msum[i-1]):msum[i] is 1:1, or simply 1.  Then your quadratic form,
> > >  E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6] %*% Sigma[1:6, 1:6] %*% t(E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6])
> > > is not working correctly in R (or nimble).  Here is an example:
> > > E <- 1:6 # E[(1+msum[i-1]):msum[i], 1:6] returns a vector of length 6, so it is something of the same type as 1:6
> > > Sigma <- diag(6)
> > > E %*% Sigma %*% t(E) # error
> > >
> > > The problem is R dynamically evaluates the types of inputs to the %*% function.  When it sees a vector, it checks whether treating it as a one-row or one-column matrix will make it conformable. e.g. both of these work:
> > > E %*% Sigma
> > > Sigma %*% E
> > >  But the default matrix for E is a one-column matrix, so t(E) is a one-row matrix, and this is non-conformable:  You are telling R which way you want it to handle E, and that way doesn't work.
> > > Sigma %*% t(E)
> > > Again, this error is occurring in R, but it is something you'll need to fix for nimble compilation to work as well.
> > > There will also be an issue in nimble when you use extents like 1:m[i] that are simply 1:1.  So for both reasons, I'd suggest separating the cases where the extent is 1:1.  You could potentially pick those out separately and declare them in a for loop with scalar operations and a dnorm instead of dmnorm.
> > >
> > > I also noticed nimbleModel is giving you a warning (at the end of its output) about multiple declarations of mu_tau.  If that is indexed only by t, it should not be in a loop with i.  You can make a separate loop over t to declare the mu_tau nodes.
> > >
> > > I also noticed, in your R code for simulating inputs, the lines like
> > > y[i,j] ~ rbinom(1, 1, 0.5)
> > > are not doing anything.  In R code, you'll want "<-" instead of "~".
> > >
> > > HTH and good luck with it.

messages.body_plain:
All,

I've put forth my best effort towards implementing the sampler, but I'm a little stuck.

Here's what I have done so far:
Implemented dMCRP (NOTE: it will only compile if you give the input argument as a vector of doubles--does not work as a vector of integers. Hopefully, this will not cause a problem since ultimately we will be sampling the z's
Created invalid rMCRP function because Nimble complained
Confirmed with 3-dim case that summing over dMCRP evaluates to 1 (so the normalizing constant is computed correctly)
Wrote some nimbleCode that uses the custom density function
Started writing the sampler based on Neal Algorithm 8 (I realize the current example is a conjugate case, but I wanted to write the non-conjugate case for generality)

What needs to be done (highlighted below in the code):
Compute the log conditional density for y_i | z_i (non-conjugate case)
Sample from the base measure for the auxiliary variables for Neal Algorithm 8.

library(nimble)
remove(list = ls())
logsumexp <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(a = double(0), b = double(0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    m <- max(a, b)
    return( log(exp(a-m) + exp(b-m)) + m )
  }
)

logsumexp_vec <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    m <- max(x)
    return( m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) )
  }
)

#' Compute log V_n(t) as in Miller and Harrison
#'
#' @param t number of partitions
#' @param n sample size
#' @param lambda mean hyperparameter for poisson prior on k-1
#' @param gamma dirichlet parameter
#' @param tol tolerance for sum
#' @return computation of log V_n(t)
logvn <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(
      t      = integer(0)
    , n      = integer(0)
    , lambda = double(0)
    , gamma  = double(0)
    , tol    = double(0, default = 1e-12)
  ) {
    returnType(double(0))
    thresh <- 1.0 - tol     ## the sum decays faster than the poisson CDF
    ## Number of partitions t must be <= n
    if ( t > n )
      return(-Inf)
    a <- 0.0      ## Previous value of log V_n(t)
    c <- -Inf     ## Computation of log V_n(t)
    k <- 1        ## counter for the sum
    p <- 0.0      ## poisson CDF calculation (to be compared with thresh)
    while ( abs(a-c) > tol | p < thresh ) {
      if ( k >= t ) {
        gamma_k <- gamma * k
        a       <- c
        b       <- lgamma(k+1) - lgamma(k-t+1) - lgamma(gamma_k + n) + lgamma(gamma_k) + dpois(k-1, lambda, 1)
        c       <- logsumexp(a, b)
      }
      p <- p + dpois(k-1, lambda, 0)
      k <- k + 1
    }
    return(c)
  }
)

nimbleUnique <- nimbleRcall(
  prototype   = function(x = double(1)) {}
  , Rfun       = "unique"
  , returnType = double(1)
)
getClusterSize <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    returnType(double(1))
    clusters    <- nimbleUnique(x)
    nclusters   <- length(clusters)
    clusterSize <- rep(0, nclusters)
    n <- length(x)
    for ( i in 1:n ) {
      for ( j in 1:nclusters ) {
        if ( x[i] == clusters[j] ) {
          clusterSize[j] <- clusterSize[j] + 1
        }
      }
    }
    return(clusterSize)
  }
)

dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(
      x = double(1)
    , size = integer(0)
    , lambda = double(0)
    , gamma = double(0)
    , tol = double(0, default = 1e-12)
    , log = integer(0, default = 0)
  ) {
    returnType(double(0))
    C <- getClusterSize(x) ## size of each partition
    t <- length(C)         ## number of parts in the partition
    ## Compute log V_n(t)
    log_vn <- logvn(t, size, lambda, gamma, tol)
    ## Compute log kernel of mass function
    logK <- 0
    ## Compute lgamma(gamma)
    lgamma_gamma <- lgamma(gamma)
    for ( j in 1:t ) {
      logK <- logK + lgamma(gamma + C[j]) - lgamma_gamma
    }
    if ( log )
      return( logK + log_vn )
    return( exp( logK + log_vn ) )
  }
)

rMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(
      n = integer(0)
    , size = integer(0)
    , lambda = double(0)
    , gamma = double(0)
    , tol = double(0, default = 1e-12)
  ) {
    returnType(double(1))
    return(rep(1, size))
  }
)

## test n = 3 case
x <- cbind( c(1, 1, 1), c(1, 1, 2), c(1, 2, 2), c(1, 2, 1), c(1, 2, 3) )
sum( apply(x, 2, dMCRP, size = 3, lambda = 3, gamma = 2) )  ## sums to 1

code <- nimbleCode({
  lambda ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
  gamma  ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
  z[1:n] ~ dMCRP(size = n, lambda, gamma, tol = 1e-12)
  nclust <- length( nimbleUnique(z[1:n]) )
  for ( k in 1:Kmax ) {
    mu[k] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 5)
  }
  for ( i in 1:n ) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[z[i]], 1)
  }
})

sampler_MFM <- nimbleFunction(
  name = 'sampler_MFM',
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    targetElements <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
    targetVar      <- model$getVarNames(nodes = target)
    n              <- length(targetElements)
    naux           <- control$naux
    parms          <- model$getParents(target)
    lambda         <- values(model, parms[1])[1]
    gamma          <- values(model, parms[2])[1]
    depvar         <- model$getDependencies(target, self = FALSE, dataOnly = TRUE, stochOnly = TRUE)
    if (is.null(control$naux))
      naux <- 3
    znew <- 1:n
    for ( j in 1:n ) {
      ## Remove observation j
      if ( j == 1 ) {
        z_mj <- z[2:n]
      } else if ( j == n ) {
        z_mj <- z[1:(n-1)]
      } else {
        z_mj <- z[c(1:j-1, (j+1):n)]
      }
      clustSize_mj  <- getClusterSize(z_mj)    ## number in each cluster after taking away obs j
      k_mj          <- length(clustSize_mj)    ## number of clusters after taking away obs j
      h_mj          <- nclust_mj + aux         ## number of total parameters incl. auxiliary
      logProbs_mj   <- rep(0, nclust_mj + h)   ## placeholder for log probabilities
      log_vn_tplus1 <- logvn(k_mj + 1)
      log_vn_t      <- logvn(k_mj)
      alpha_mj      <- exp( log(gamma) + log_vn_tplus1 - log_vn_t ) ## concentration parameter
      ## loop through number of clusters + aux variables
      for ( k in 1:k_mj ) {
        ## REPLACE ... WITH LOG LIKELIHOOD BASED ON THIS CLUSTER AND DEPVAR[j]
        logprobs_mj[k] <- log(clustSize_mj[k]) - log(n - 1 + alpha_mj) + ...
      }
      for ( k in (k_mj+1):h_mj ) {
        ## REPLACE ... WITH A DRAW FROM BASE MEASURE
        ...

        ## REPLACE ... WITH LOG LIKELIHOOD BASED ON THIS CLUSTER AND DEPVAR[j]
        logprobs_mj[k] <- log(alpha_mj) - log(naux) - log(n - 1 + alpha_mj) + ...
      }
      znew[j] <- rcat( n = 1, prob = exp(logprobs_mj) )
    }
    model[[target]] <<- znew
    model$calculate(target)
    nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = target, logProb = TRUE)
  }
)

## SAMPLE DATA
n <- 20
K <- 2
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
y <- numeric(n)
y[z==1] <- rnorm(sum(z==1), 2, 1)
y[z==0] <- rnorm(sum(z==0), -2, 1)
Kmax <- 5
mod <- nimbleModel(
  code
  , constants = list(n = n, Kmax = Kmax)
  , data  = list('y' = y)
  , inits = list('z' = rep(1, n), 'mu' = rnorm(Kmax, mean = 0, sd = 0.5), 'lambda' = 1, 'gamma' = 1)
)
cmod <- compileNimble(mod)
conf <- configureMCMC(mod, monitors = c('nclust', 'lambda', 'gamma', 'mu'))

> Hi Hanah,

> 2) Please provide nb, nbrs, and start as part of inits not as part of constants. That's what the (hard to interpret) error message is trying to indicate.

> > > Hi Hanah,
> > >
> > > The specific issue is that you can't use arbitrary R code in defining your model (please see Section 5.2.5 of our manual). In particular, there's various R functions in these lines that won't work (rep, seq_along, as.numeric, tapply):
> > >
> > > g <- rep(seq_along(vec1), vec1)
> > > sumld<--as.numeric(tapply(lamda[vec2], g, sum))
> > >
> > > However, you can do this with some additional work. Your case is similar to another discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/b8G-1MtTm-c/m/smrwlsTUBAAJ> we had on the users group a while back. The basic idea is that you need to do the indexing as part of a nimbleFunction (because we don't support syntax like `sum(u[idx[1:4]])` directly in model code).
> > >
> > > Outside of your model code, write a nimbleFunction that does the mean calculation:
> > >
> > > mymean <- nimbleFunction(
> > >     run = function(lambda = double(1), nbrs = double(1), start = double(1), nb = double(1), i = double(0)) {
> > >         return(mean(lambda[nbrs[start[i]:(start[i]+nb[i]-1)]])
> > >         returnType(double(0))
> > >     }
> > > )
> > >
> > > Then in model code:
> > >
> > > u[i] <- mymean(lambda, nbrs, start, nb, i)
> > >
> > > You'd need to provide nbrs, idx and nb as constants. 'nbrs' should be vector containing the deltas, all strung together in a single vector. 'start' should be a vector indicating the first delta for each i.  Suppose that the delta_1 is {1,3} and delta_2 is {1,7,11}, and delta_3 is {2, 4} and so forth. Then 'start' is {1,3,6,...}.
> > >
> > > Alternatively, your spatial formulation is similar to a CAR model, so you may want to consider that instead. See Chapter 9 of our manual and this example <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/CAR.html>.
> > >
> > > -chris
> > >

> > > > I define the model in NIMBLE as:

> > > >   for(i in 1:N) {

> > > >     log(theta[i]) <- alpha + u[i]
> > > >     y[i] ~ dpois(theta[i]*E[i])

> > > > L<-length(vec2)
> > > > N = nrow(data)

I'll chime in here--I've been having the exact same issue, with nimble and with another (bespoke) package I've written.  It took me a few hours of rabbit-holing, but I found that R 4.2+ seems to have a problem with multi-coring (sorry, I didn't save the links).  In my case, it was really weird--I'd run a multi-core job in R (nimble or my own package), and it would work and shut down the workers just fine.  Then I'd run it again in the same R session and get the error Sanjib noted (nimble only, my own function had a different error message).  I was not changing anything in the function used by the workers itself.

I tried using the parallel package (as per the instructions Sanjib linked to), futures/doFutures packages, restarting R, restarting and updating all packages, manually deleting the parallel, etc. packages then re-installing, and so on, but I'd still get the same behavior.  It was really strange, and left me unable to use some functions in MC mode.

What I found seem to work was simply re-installing R (same version--4.2.1).  Also, I have an intuition that any calls to setwd() (outside the worker code) may have made things go awry, but I'm not sure of that. There is nothing in the worker code that needs access to a folder I created, though.

It's not a great solution, but it's working for me at the moment.

Adam

Hi Hanah,

Yes, good point. Those values are conceptually constants in their role in the model.

As I was debugging your code, it looks like I got confused at some point and thought that for some reason that nimble needed those to be provided in inits for internal reasons, but I see now that it works if you provide them in constants (or in inits is fine too). For vector constants like these, we do create a model variable for them, but that's an internal detail not all that relevant here.

-chris

> > > > The specific issue is that you can't use arbitrary R code in defining your model (please see Section 5.2.5 of our manual). In particular, there's various R functions in these lines that won't work (rep, seq_along, as.numeric, tapply):
> > > >
> > > > g <- rep(seq_along(vec1), vec1)
> > > > sumld<--as.numeric(tapply(lamda[vec2], g, sum))
> > > >
> > > > However, you can do this with some additional work. Your case is similar to another discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/b8G-1MtTm-c/m/smrwlsTUBAAJ> we had on the users group a while back. The basic idea is that you need to do the indexing as part of a nimbleFunction (because we don't support syntax like `sum(u[idx[1:4]])` directly in model code).
> > > >
> > > > Outside of your model code, write a nimbleFunction that does the mean calculation:
> > > >
> > > > mymean <- nimbleFunction(
> > > >     run = function(lambda = double(1), nbrs = double(1), start = double(1), nb = double(1), i = double(0)) {
> > > >         return(mean(lambda[nbrs[start[i]:(start[i]+nb[i]-1)]])
> > > >         returnType(double(0))
> > > >     }
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > Then in model code:
> > > >
> > > > u[i] <- mymean(lambda, nbrs, start, nb, i)
> > > >
> > > > You'd need to provide nbrs, idx and nb as constants. 'nbrs' should be vector containing the deltas, all strung together in a single vector. 'start' should be a vector indicating the first delta for each i.  Suppose that the delta_1 is {1,3} and delta_2 is {1,7,11}, and delta_3 is {2, 4} and so forth. Then 'start' is {1,3,6,...}.
> > > >
> > > > Alternatively, your spatial formulation is similar to a CAR model, so you may want to consider that instead. See Chapter 9 of our manual and this example <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/CAR.html>.
> > > >
> > > > -chris
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Jul 15, 2022 at 11:04 AM Hanah <hnhn0...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > >
> > > > > I am fitting a spatial model as follows:

> > > > >   sumld<--as.numeric(tapply(lamda[vec2], g, sum))
> > > > >
> > > > >   for(i in 1:N) {
> > > > >     u[i]<-1/nb[i]*sumld[i]
> > > > >     log(theta[i]) <- alpha + u[i]
> > > > >     y[i] ~ dpois(theta[i]*E[i])
> > > > >   }
> > > > > }
> > > > > )
> > > > >   ####  Data

> > > > > vec1<-vec1  #this gives the number of neighbors for each area

> > > > > L<-length(vec2)
> > > > > N = nrow(data)

> > > > >               u=rep(0,N))
> > > > > params <- c("alpha", "tau", "u","lamda") # Params
> > > > >
> > > > > #### Create the model
> > > > > MR <- nimbleModel(
> > > > >   code = model_code,
> > > > >   name = "MR",
> > > > >   constants = nb.const,
> > > > >   data = nb.data,

messages.subject: Re: Aggregate simulated daily values to match monthly data
messages.subject_clean: Aggregate simulated daily values to match monthly data
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thanks so much for taking the time to send this. I took some time to look through it, but eventually had to conclude it was beyond my fairly rudimentary understanding of statistics! I therefore thought I would start with what seemed like a more basic solution to achieve integer simulation values in order to use a binomial distribution to map cases to infections. My theory was that I could just swap the ODE solver to a discrete tau-leaping algorithm (I went for the package adaptivetau). However, while I am able to simulate data successfully using the ssa.adaptivetau function, when I use it as a NimbleFunction, I start getting input errors (despite the fact that the inputs should be exactly the same?) I was wondering if you could think of any fundamental reasons why this approach wouldn't work (both technically in Nimble and mathematically)? The problem appears to be with the rate function, which is used as an argument within the NimbleFunction. I think maybe I need to declare it as an argument within the nimbleRcall() function, but I'm not sure if that's possible? Can you think of an alternative solution? (Hopefully this makes sense with the code!). As always, your input is much appreciated!

Here is the code:
library(nimble)
library(dplyr)
library(adaptivetau)

##################################### FUNCTIONS #################################################
#Tau-leap rate function
rate_function <- function(x, p, t) {
  return(c(x["I"]*p$e, #Bacteria Birth
           0.33, #Bacteria death
           p$mu * (x["S"] + x["I"]), # Human birth
           p$mu * x["S"], #Susceptible death
           p$a * (x["B"] / (x["B"] + 10**6)) * x["S"], # Infection
           p$r * x["I"])) #Infective death
}

#Convert from who-knows-what timescale to daily
get_daily <- function(results,num_days){
  df <- as.data.frame(results)
  df$day <- ceiling(df$time)
  daily <- data.frame(day = 1:num_days, S = NA, I = NA, B = NA)
  for(i in 1:num_days){
    day <- df %>%
      filter(day == i)
    if(nrow(day) > 0){
      daily[i,2:4] <- tail(day[,2:4],1)
    } else {
      daily[i,2:4] <- daily[i-1,2:4]
    }
  }
  return(daily)
}

rate_function <- function(x, p, t) {
  return(c(x["I"]*p$e, #Bacteria Birth
           0.33, #Bacteria death
           p$mu * (x["S"] + x["I"]), # Human birth
           p$mu * x["S"], #Susceptible death
           p$a * (x["B"] / (x["B"] + 10**6)) * x["S"], # Infection
           p$r * x["I"])) #Infective death
}

##Simulate Data
SIB_daily <- function(z_init, theta){
  #Transition matrix
  transitions = ssa.maketrans(names(z_init),
                                 rbind('B', +1), # Bacteria birth
                                 rbind('B', -1), # Bacteria death
                                 rbind('S', +1), # Human birth
                                 rbind('S', -1), #Susceptible death
                                 rbind('S', -1, 'I', +1), #Infection
                                 rbind('I', -1) #Infective death
  )

  num_days = 300
  theta_list <- as.list(theta)
  results =ssa.adaptivetau(z_init, transitions, rate_function, theta_list, tf= num_days)
  daily = get_daily(results,num_days)
  return(daily)
}

#Remove intial values and day column for Nimble
SIB_daily_nim <- function(z_init, theta){
  SIB_daily_nim <- SIB_daily(z_init,theta)[-1,2:4]
  return(as.matrix(SIB_daily_nim))
}

nimODE <- nimbleRcall(function(z_init = integer(1), theta = double(1)){}, Rfun = 'SIB_daily_nim',
                      returnType = integer(2))

##################################### INITIAL SET UP ###########################################
#Parameters
theta <- c(
  a = 1,
  e = 10,
  r = 0.2,
  mu = 0.0001
)

#Set initial values
N = 10000
I0 = 10
B0 = 0
S0 = N - I0
num_days = 300
z_init <- c(S = S0, I = I0, B = B0)

#Transitions
SIB_daily_sim <- SIB_daily(z_init, theta) #Simulate 'true' values
daily_cases <- rbinom(n = nrow(SIB_daily_sim), size = SIB_daily_sim$I, p = 0.3)[-1] #Simulate reported cases

###################################### NIMBLE MODEL #################################################
Model <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:n){
    y[i] ~ dbin(prob = p, size = z[i,2])
  }
  z[1:n,1:3] <- nimODE(z_init=z_init[1:3],theta=theta[1:4])
  ## Priors
  p ~ dbeta(shape1 = 1.3, shape2 = 5) #P
  theta[1] ~ T(dnorm(0,5),0,) #dgamma(3,0.6)        #a
  theta[2] ~ T(dnorm(0,5),0,) #dgamma(10,1)         #e
  theta[3] ~ T(dnorm(0,5),0,) #dgamma(3, 0.06)      #r
  theta[4] ~ T(dnorm(0,0.1),0,)
})
Consts <- list(n = num_days - 1)
nimbleData <- list(y=daily_cases,z_init=z_init)
inits <- list(theta=c(1,1,1,0.001),p=0.3)
nimbleModel <- nimbleModel(code=Model, name='nimbleModel', constants = Consts, data = nimbleData,inits = inits)
MCMCconfig <- configureMCMC(nimbleModel,monitors=c("theta","p"))

modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(MCMCconfig)
compiled_model <- compileNimble(nimbleModel, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

compiled_model_MCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = nimbleModel)
results <- runMCMC(compiled_model_MCMC, niter = 50000, nburnin = 30000, nchains = 1, thin=10,
                   inits=inits, progressBar = T, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T)

Thank you!
Debbie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ethan,

Looks like you've made some good progress. Here are some suggestions:

1) You'll need your sampler_MFM to have a setup function and a run function. The actual sampling calculations need to be in the run function (this looks like the stuff starting with 'for(j in 1:n)' in your code).
The sampler_CRP code (in BNP_samplers.R) may be helpful, but the setup code there is quite complicated because we need to handle all sorts of model structures a user might pass. So you might also look at some simpler samplers (in MCMC_samplers.R to get a better sense for what is in setup() and what is in run().

2) You'll need a 'reset' method for sampler_MFM. You can just use the 'dummy' one shown for sampler_CRP.

3) As far as the computations, I presume you know what calcs to do for '## REPLACE ... WITH LOG LIKELIHOOD BASED ON THIS CLUSTER AND DEPVAR[j]'.

For ## REPLACE ... WITH A DRAW FROM BASE MEASURE',  you'll need to use the 'simulate' method applied to the cluster parameters for the given cluster. You might be able
to determine the cluster parameters in the setup code such that this works for any model. We do this in sampler_CRP, but it is complicated graph stuff. So an easier alternative is to have the user of sampler_MFM pass in a vector of the node names for the cluster parameters as part of the control list. Then you can grab those in the setup code and use them in the run code.

4) You'll need to set `z <- model[[target]]` early on in the run code.

5) At the end of run code, you need to make sure that you copy the current values of the model and all logProbs into the mvSaved modelValues (see various samplers for an example of this). This means that you'll also need to make sure that you've updated any deterministic dependencies of any model nodes that you changed in the sampling in sampler_MFM as well as any logProbs for dependencies of any model nodes that you changed (including logProbs of the changed nodes themselves). In sampler_CRP you'll see we do this in the last couple lines of run().

HTH. Happy to iterate further as you work on it.

-chris

messages.subject_clean: Sampling (out of sample) from posterior predictive distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a geostatistical model and want to sample from the posterior predictive distribution at a new set of locations. So far, the only way I could do it was by setting an "augmented" model with NAs at the locations at which I want to sample from this posterior predictive distribution. However, this approach is not ideal for (at least) two reasons:
1) it affects the mixing of the chains
2) what if I don't know the regions where I want these new samples a priori?

Are there any other ways of doing it?
An option, if possible, would be to increase the dimension of some nodes after running the MCMC and then simulate the data from the model. I don't know how to do it though.
I have looked into the documentation and the email list and have not found anything helpful in this regard yet.

Any help or resources are very much appreciated.

P.s.: I have attached a (simplified) reproducible toy example to make what I'm trying to say clearer.

Thank you in advance.
Best,
Lucas.

messages.subject_clean: Sampling (out of sample) from posterior predictive distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lucas,

Right, you generally don't want to add the predictive nodes into the model for the reasons you say. We have an open to-do item to detect such predictive nodes and have their sampling be done only in 'predictive mode' without influencing the posterior sampling of everything else, but it's not something we've been able to put time into yet.

We have a simple example of posterior predictive sampling here <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/posterior_predictive.html> that shows simulation into nodes that already exist in the model.

To do what you want, one approach would be:

1) Run the MCMC on the original model (using only the observed locations)
2) Set up a 'full' model that includes declarations for the spatial process at the original locations and for the spatial process at the new locations conditional on the original locations. You'll need to code up the conditional multivariate normal calculations for your declaration for the new locations. (You could use definition-time if-then-else to avoid having to write the model code twice, but that's a minor thing.)
3) Use the ideas from #1 to put the sampled values (process and relevant hyperparameters) into the full model and simulate process values at the new locations conditional on the posterior samples.

Happy to iterate if you have questions or get stuck.

-chris

Hey Chris,

Firstly, thanks for your help and prompt response!
At first sight, I thought it had worked, however, I'm not sure.
Here go some thoughts:
1) the if-then-else approach has not worked. The reason is that is says the "cov_pred" matrix is not positive definite when trying to calculate its Cholesky decomposition. I believe it might be due to numerical problems.
2) the way I created the function to calculate the predictions we pass a "target" node and the function uses `model$getParents` to track the parents of the target node. What I notice is that the grand-parents of the node are not being tracked by that function. For instance, "lifted" nodes needed to simulate `s_pred` (which is needed to predict the new data points) do not appear when I call `model$getParents` at the positions of "y" to which I want to calculate the predictions. Would "simulate" automatically deal with those lifted nodes?
3) when I plotted the predicted (posterior mean of the predictive distribution at each point t) vs the true it does not look right.

Any thoughts?
Also, is there a "chol2inv" function in Nimble?

Thank you agagin.
Best,
Lucas.

On Tue, Aug 9, 2022 at 7:58 PM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Lucas,
>
> Right, you generally don't want to add the predictive nodes into the model for the reasons you say. We have an open to-do item to detect such predictive nodes and have their sampling be done only in 'predictive mode' without influencing the posterior sampling of everything else, but it's not something we've been able to put time into yet.
>
> We have a simple example of posterior predictive sampling here <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/posterior_predictive.html> that shows simulation into nodes that already exist in the model.
>
> To do what you want, one approach would be:
>
> 1) Run the MCMC on the original model (using only the observed locations)
> 2) Set up a 'full' model that includes declarations for the spatial process at the original locations and for the spatial process at the new locations conditional on the original locations. You'll need to code up the conditional multivariate normal calculations for your declaration for the new locations. (You could use definition-time if-then-else to avoid having to write the model code twice, but that's a minor thing.)
> 3) Use the ideas from #1 to put the sampled values (process and relevant hyperparameters) into the full model and simulate process values at the new locations conditional on the posterior samples.
>
> Happy to iterate if you have questions or get stuck.
>
> -chris
>
>
>
>
>

> > Any help or resources are very much appreciated.

> >
> > Thank you in advance.
> > Best,
> > Lucas.

messages.subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.subject_clean: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.

    #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
    library(parallel)
    library(coda)
    set.seed(3)
    cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
    clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))

    for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
      set.seed(j)
      init <- inits()
      clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
    }

    out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
      library(nimble)
      library(coda)

      model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",

                           constants = constants, data = data,

                           inits = init)
      Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
      modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)

      modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)

      modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
      CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)

      CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
      return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
    })

    ## Check convergence ##
    out2 <- out1
    out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
    out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
    out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
    #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
    library(mcmcOutput)
    #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
    mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
    sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
    sumTab <- sumTab %>%
      as_tibble() %>%
      mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
      select(Parameter, mean:f)
    #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
    ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
                       !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
                       !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
                       !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
                       !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
    mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
    #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()

    ## If has not converged, continue sampling

    n.reruns <- 0
    while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
      out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
        CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
        return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
      })

      n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
      print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
      if(n.reruns == 1) {
        nb2 <- nb + nb
        ni2 <- ni + ni
      } else {
        nb2 <- nb2 + nb
        ni2 <- ni2 + ni
      }
      out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
      out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
      out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))

      mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
      sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
      sumTab <- sumTab %>%
        as_tibble() %>%
        mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
        select(Parameter, mean:f)
      #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
      mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
      gc(verbose = F)
    }
    #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~#

> hi Dan,

>
> One other note is that the approach in that example relies on simply setting different seeds for the different chains. While this is probably safe, it is possible that the random numbers generated for one chain could partially overlap the random numbers generated for another chain. messages.body_plain:
Hi Lucas,

1) The positive-definiteness is a numerical issue that should be unrelated to getting if-then-else to work. It works if you just define the predictive model separately?
2) No, simulate won't automatically deal with the graph structure. You need to make sure that you are telling simulate exactly what needs to be simulated, including all lifted nodes. I think what you need is "getParents("s_pred[1:10]", determOnly = TRUE)' and then concatenate "s_pred[1:10]" onto that, since with determOnly, it won't include 's_pred' since it is stoch. All the stochastic parents(phi, tau, s) should be filled with values from the original MCMC. ("10" here is just a placeholder...)
3) This likely relates at least in part to #2. It looks like you might be simulating 's' in the predictive sampling when you should be conditioning on its values from the initial MCMC.
4) No, there's not a chol2inv function, though you could implement the equivalent using chol(), forwardsolve() and backsolve().

Side note: your `code_pred` doesn't need to include 'y' since it's not involved in the predictive simulation of s_pred.

-chris

> > 3) when I plotted the predicted (posterior mean of the predictive distribution at each point t) vs the true it does not look right.

We have an open to-do item to detect such predictive nodes and have their sampling be done only in 'predictive mode' without influencing the posterior sampling of everything else, but it's not something we've been able to put time into yet.
> > >
> > > We have a simple example of posterior predictive sampling here <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/posterior_predictive.html> that shows simulation into nodes that already exist in the model.

> > > To do what you want, one approach would be:
> > >
> > > 1) Run the MCMC on the original model (using only the observed locations)
> > > 2) Set up a 'full' model that includes declarations for the spatial process at the original locations and for the spatial process at the new locations conditional on the original locations. You'll need to code up the conditional multivariate normal calculations for your declaration for the new locations. (You could use definition-time if-then-else to avoid having to write the model code twice, but that's a minor thing.)
> > > 3) Use the ideas from #1 to put the sampled values (process and relevant hyperparameters) into the full model and simulate process values at the new locations conditional on the posterior samples.

Hi Ethan,

I'm not quite understanding. When you call $simulate, that will put values into the model in the node(s) that contain the cluster parameters. And then at the end you are copying from the model to mvSaved, so you are storing the new cluster parameter values. In your code comment you mention the value of a parameter for an index, but isn't this just obtained by looking in the appropriate place in the node(s) containing the cluster parameters?

More generally, I think you can follow the logic of what is done in our CRP_sampler.

(Note - I'm responding quickly without spending the time to think this through carefully...)

-chris

> logsumexp <- nimbleFunction(

>     returnType(double(0))
>     m <- max(a, b)
>     return( log(exp(a-m) + exp(b-m)) + m )
>   }
> )
>
> logsumexp_vec <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = double(1)) {
>     returnType(double(0))
>     m <- max(x)
>     return( m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) )
>   }
> )
>
> #' Compute log V_n(t) as in Miller and Harrison
> #'
> #' @param t number of partitions
> #' @param n sample size
> #' @param lambda mean hyperparameter for poisson prior on k-1
> #' @param gamma dirichlet parameter
> #' @param tol tolerance for sum
> #' @return computation of log V_n(t)
> logvn <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(
>       t      = integer(0)
>     , n      = integer(0)
>     , lambda = double(0)
>     , gamma  = double(0)
>     , tol    = double(0, default = 1e-12)
>   ) {
>     returnType(double(0))
>     thresh <- 1.0 - tol     ## the sum decays faster than the poisson CDF
>     ## Number of partitions t must be <= n
>     if ( t > n )
>       return(-Inf)
>     a <- 0.0      ## Previous value of log V_n(t)
>     c <- -Inf     ## Computation of log V_n(t)
>     k <- 1        ## counter for the sum
>     p <- 0.0      ## poisson CDF calculation (to be compared with thresh)
>     while ( abs(a-c) > tol | p < thresh ) {
>       if ( k >= t ) {
>         gamma_k <- gamma * k
>         a       <- c
>         b       <- lgamma(k+1) - lgamma(k-t+1) - lgamma(gamma_k + n) + lgamma(gamma_k) + dpois(k-1, lambda, 1)
>         c       <- logsumexp(a, b)
>       }
>       p <- p + dpois(k-1, lambda, 0)
>       k <- k + 1
>     }
>     return(c)
>   }
> )
>
> #' Function to get sizes of clusters
> #'
> #' @param x vector of cluster membership
> #' @param max_components maximum number of components
> #'
> #' @return a vector giving sizes of clusters whose elements are 1:max_components
> getClusterSizes <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = double(1), max_components = integer(0)) {
>     returnType(double(1))
>     res <- rep(0, max_components)
>     n   <- length(x)
>     for ( i in 1:n ) {
>       res[x[i]] <- res[x[i]] + 1
>     }
>     return(res)
>   }
> )
>
>
> #' Nimble list for cluster membership
> membershipList <- nimbleList(
>   empty = double(1), nonempty = double(1)
> )
> #' Function to get the indexes of the empty and non-empty clusters
> #'
> #' @param x an object returned from getClusterSizes
> #' @return a list of two elements:
> #' \itemize{
> #'    \item "nonempty" a vector of cluster indexes that are nonempty
> #'    \item "empty" a vector of cluster indexes that are empty
> #' }
> getClusterIndexes <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = double(1)) {
>     res <- membershipList$new()
>     returnType(membershipList())
>     max_components <- length(x)
>     for ( i in 1:max_components ) {
>       if ( x[i] > 0 ) {
>         res$nonempty <- c(res$nonempty, i)
>       } else {
>         res$empty <- c(res$empty, i)
>       }
>     }
>     return(res)
>   }
> )
>
>
> #' Mass function for modified CRP
> #'
> #' Computes the mass function for the modified CRP of Miller
> #'
> #' @param x vector giving cluster membership
> #' @param size length of x
> #' @param lambda parameter for poisson prior on (number of components - 1)
> #' @param gamma parameter for Dirichlet prior on membership probability
> #' @param tol tolerance for computing log normalizing constant
> #' @param log whether to return on log scale
> #'
> #' @return a scalar giving the mass function for the cluster membership
> dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(
>       x = double(1)
>     , size = integer()
>     , lambda = double(0)
>     , gamma = double(0)
>     , tol = double(0, default = 1e-12)
>     , log = integer(0, default = 0)
>   ) {
>     returnType(double(0))
>     classSizes <- getClusterSizes(x, max(x))     ## size of each class
>     clustList  <- getClusterIndexes(classSizes)  ## list of empty/nonempty indices
>     C <- classSizes[clustList$nonempty]          ## vector giving sizes of each nonempty cluster
>     t <- length(C)                               ## number of parts in the partition
>     ## Compute log V_n(t)
>     log_vn <- logvn(t, length(x), lambda, gamma, tol)
>     ## Compute log kernel of mass function
>     logK <- 0
>     ## Compute lgamma(gamma)
>     lgamma_gamma <- lgamma(gamma)
>     for ( j in 1:t ) {
>       logK <- logK + lgamma(gamma + C[j]) - lgamma_gamma
>     }
>     if ( log )
>       return( logK + log_vn )
>     return( exp( logK + log_vn ) )
>   }
> )
>
>
>
> #' Dummy random number generator for MCRP

>       stop("Number of auxiliary parameters must be fewer than max number of components.")
>     lognaux <- log(naux)
>   }
>   , run = function() {
>     ## Get current cluster membership
>     z <- model[[target]]
>
>     ## Create copy of cluster-specific parameters
>     yparmClustCopy <- values(model, yparmsClust)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ann

You might check the output of the  shell command-line call
xcode-select -p

If the output doesn't say something like  /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools, but instead says ..../Developer, you probably need to set it, e.g.,

sudo xcode-select -s /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools
See SO <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57494601/clang-cant-compile-basic-header-files-like-iostream-in-macos> question.

Worth a try.
D.

messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

Admittedly, I found the CRP_sampler a little difficult to read.

The logic was as follows:
Simulate to obtain a draw from the base measure: theta = (theta_1*, ..., theta_{max_components}*)
Compute log probability for each cluster from k = 1, ..., max_components, max_components + 1, ..., max_components + naux
Draw z
If z corresponds to an existing cluster:
replace all the parameters back to their original values
If z corresponds to a new cluster:
change the value to the index corresponding to the first empty cluster
Set the parameters for the empty cluster to the draw from part (1)

On Tuesday, August 16, 2022 at 1:42:18 PM UTC-4 Christopher Paciorek wrote:
> Hi Ethan,
>
> I'm not quite understanding. When you call $simulate, that will put values into the model in the node(s) that contain the cluster parameters. And then at the end you are copying from the model to mvSaved, so you are storing the new cluster parameter values. In your code comment you mention the value of a parameter for an index, but isn't this just obtained by looking in the appropriate place in the node(s) containing the cluster parameters?
>
> More generally, I think you can follow the logic of what is done in our CRP_sampler.
>
> (Note - I'm responding quickly without spending the time to think this through carefully...)
>
> -chris
>
> On Tue, Aug 16, 2022 at 10:09 AM E A <ethanm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hey Chris,
> >
> > I've been hard at work on this implementation, and here is what I have come up with. The remaining piece of the puzzle is storing the values of the parameters for the newly-defined clusters.
> >
> > logsumexp <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(a = double(0), b = double(0)) {
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >     m <- max(a, b)
> >     return( log(exp(a-m) + exp(b-m)) + m )
> >   }
> > )
> >
> > logsumexp_vec <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(x = double(1)) {
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >     m <- max(x)
> >     return( m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) )
> >   }
> > )
> >
> > #' Compute log V_n(t) as in Miller and Harrison
> > #'
> > #' @param t number of partitions
> > #' @param n sample size
> > #' @param lambda mean hyperparameter for poisson prior on k-1
> > #' @param gamma dirichlet parameter
> > #' @param tol tolerance for sum
> > #' @return computation of log V_n(t)
> > logvn <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(
> >       t      = integer(0)
> >     , n      = integer(0)
> >     , lambda = double(0)
> >     , gamma  = double(0)
> >     , tol    = double(0, default = 1e-12)
> >   ) {
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >     thresh <- 1.0 - tol     ## the sum decays faster than the poisson CDF
> >     ## Number of partitions t must be <= n
> >     if ( t > n )
> >       return(-Inf)
> >     a <- 0.0      ## Previous value of log V_n(t)
> >     c <- -Inf     ## Computation of log V_n(t)
> >     k <- 1        ## counter for the sum
> >     p <- 0.0      ## poisson CDF calculation (to be compared with thresh)
> >     while ( abs(a-c) > tol | p < thresh ) {
> >       if ( k >= t ) {
> >         gamma_k <- gamma * k
> >         a       <- c
> >         b       <- lgamma(k+1) - lgamma(k-t+1) - lgamma(gamma_k + n) + lgamma(gamma_k) + dpois(k-1, lambda, 1)
> >         c       <- logsumexp(a, b)
> >       }
> >       p <- p + dpois(k-1, lambda, 0)
> >       k <- k + 1
> >     }
> >     return(c)
> >   }
> > )
> >
> > #' Function to get sizes of clusters
> > #'
> > #' @param x vector of cluster membership
> > #' @param max_components maximum number of components
> > #'
> > #' @return a vector giving sizes of clusters whose elements are 1:max_components
> > getClusterSizes <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(x = double(1), max_components = integer(0)) {
> >     returnType(double(1))
> >     res <- rep(0, max_components)
> >     n   <- length(x)
> >     for ( i in 1:n ) {
> >       res[x[i]] <- res[x[i]] + 1
> >     }
> >     return(res)
> >   }
> > )
> >
> >
> > #' Nimble list for cluster membership
> > membershipList <- nimbleList(
> >   empty = double(1), nonempty = double(1)
> > )
> > #' Function to get the indexes of the empty and non-empty clusters
> > #'
> > #' @param x an object returned from getClusterSizes
> > #' @return a list of two elements:
> > #' \itemize{
> > #'    \item "nonempty" a vector of cluster indexes that are nonempty
> > #'    \item "empty" a vector of cluster indexes that are empty
> > #' }
> > getClusterIndexes <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(x = double(1)) {
> >     res <- membershipList$new()
> >     returnType(membershipList())
> >     max_components <- length(x)
> >     for ( i in 1:max_components ) {
> >       if ( x[i] > 0 ) {
> >         res$nonempty <- c(res$nonempty, i)
> >       } else {
> >         res$empty <- c(res$empty, i)
> >       }
> >     }
> >     return(res)
> >   }
> > )
> >
> >
> > #' Mass function for modified CRP
> > #'
> > #' Computes the mass function for the modified CRP of Miller
> > #'
> > #' @param x vector giving cluster membership
> > #' @param size length of x
> > #' @param lambda parameter for poisson prior on (number of components - 1)
> > #' @param gamma parameter for Dirichlet prior on membership probability
> > #' @param tol tolerance for computing log normalizing constant
> > #' @param log whether to return on log scale
> > #'
> > #' @return a scalar giving the mass function for the cluster membership
> > dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(
> >       x = double(1)
> >     , size = integer()
> >     , lambda = double(0)
> >     , gamma = double(0)
> >     , tol = double(0, default = 1e-12)
> >     , log = integer(0, default = 0)
> >   ) {
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >     classSizes <- getClusterSizes(x, max(x))     ## size of each class
> >     clustList  <- getClusterIndexes(classSizes)  ## list of empty/nonempty indices
> >     C <- classSizes[clustList$nonempty]          ## vector giving sizes of each nonempty cluster
> >     t <- length(C)                               ## number of parts in the partition
> >     ## Compute log V_n(t)
> >     log_vn <- logvn(t, length(x), lambda, gamma, tol)
> >     ## Compute log kernel of mass function
> >     logK <- 0
> >     ## Compute lgamma(gamma)
> >     lgamma_gamma <- lgamma(gamma)
> >     for ( j in 1:t ) {
> >       logK <- logK + lgamma(gamma + C[j]) - lgamma_gamma
> >     }
> >     if ( log )
> >       return( logK + log_vn )
> >     return( exp( logK + log_vn ) )
> >   }
> > )
> >
> >
> >
> > #' Dummy random number generator for MCRP
> > rMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(
> >       n = integer(0)
> >     , size = integer(0)
> >     , lambda = double(0)
> >     , gamma = double(0)
> >     , tol = double(0, default = 1e-12)
> >   ) {
> >     returnType(double(1))
> >     return(rep(1, size))
> >   }
> > )
> >
> > sampler_MFM <- nimbleFunction(
> >   name = 'sampler_MFM',
> >   contains = sampler_BASE,
> >   setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
> >     targetElements  <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE)
> >     n               <- length(targetElements)
> >     zparms          <- model$getParents(target)
> >     lambda          <- values(model, zparms[1])[1]   ## Poisson parameter
> >     gamma           <- values(model, zparms[2])[1]   ## Dirichlet parameter
> >     ## Get names of parameters for response variable
> >     yvar            <- model$getDependencies(target, self = FALSE, dataOnly = TRUE, stochOnly = TRUE)
> >     yparmsNames     <- model$getParents(yvar, stochOnly = TRUE, omit = target)
> >     yparmsNames     <- model$getVarNames(nodes = yparmsNames)
> >     ## get number of components in mixture model
> >     max_components <- 0
> >     yparmsFixed    <- NULL
> >     yparmsClust    <- NULL
> >     for ( i in 1:length(yparmsNames) ) {
> >       yparmsExpanded <- model$expandNodeNames(yparmsNames[i])
> >       if ( length(yparmsExpanded) > 1  ) {
> >         max_components <- max(max_components, length(model$expandNodeNames(yparmsNames[i])) )
> >         yparmsClust <- c(yparmsClust, yparmsNames[i])
> >       } else {
> >         yparmsFixed <- c(yparmsFixed, yparmsNames[i])
> >       }
> >     }
> >     naux  <- control$naux
> >     if (is.null(control$naux))
> >       naux <- min(3, max_components)
> >     if ( naux > max_components )
> >       stop("Number of auxiliary parameters must be fewer than max number of components.")
> >     lognaux <- log(naux)
> >   }
> >   , run = function() {
> >     ## Get current cluster membership
> >     z <- model[[target]]
> >
> >     ## Create copy of cluster-specific parameters
> >     yparmClustCopy <- values(model, yparmsClust)
> >
> >     for ( j in 1:n ) {
> >       ## Remove observation j
> >       if ( j == 1 ) {
> >         z_mj <- z[2:n]
> >       } else if ( j == n ) {
> >         z_mj <- z[1:(n-1)]
> >       } else {
> >         z_mj <- z[c(1:(j-1), (j+1):n)]
> >       }
> >       ## number in each cluster after taking away obs j
> >       clustSize_mj     <- getClusterSizes(z_mj, max_components)  ## cluster sizes
> >       clustIndexes_mj  <- getClusterIndexes( clustSize_mj )      ## list giving which clusters are empty / non-empty
> >       clustEmpty_mj    <- clustIndexes_mj$empty                  ## indices of empty clusters
> >       clustNonempty_mj <- clustIndexes_mj$nonempty               ## indices of non-empty clusters
> >       k_mj             <- length(clustNonempty_mj)               ## number of filled clusters after taking away obs j
> >       logProbs_mj_cl   <- rep(-Inf, max_components)              ## placeholder for log likelihood for components
> >       logProbs_mj_aux  <- rep(-Inf, naux)                        ## placeholder for log likelihood for auxiliary
> >       log_vn_tplus1    <- logvn(k_mj + 1, n, lambda, gamma)      ## logvn function
> >       log_vn_t         <- logvn(k_mj, n, lambda, gamma)          ## logvn function
> >       logalpha_mj      <- log(gamma) + log_vn_tplus1 - log_vn_t  ## log concentration parameter for MFM
> >       alpha_mj         <- exp(logalpha_mj)                       ## concentration param for MFM
> >       logden_mj        <- log(n - 1 + alpha_mj)                  ## log denominator for cluster probs
> >       logProbNew_mj    <- logalpha_mj - lognaux - logden_mj      ## log probability of being in new cluster excluding likelihood
> >
> >       ## loop through number of clusters + aux variables
> >       for ( k in clustNonempty_mj ) {
> >         ## Temporarily change cluster membership to compute log probability
> >         model[[target]][j] <- k
> >
> >         ## Compute log probability of being in cluster k
> >         logProbs_mj_cl[k] <- log(clustSize_mj[k]) - logden_mj + model$calculate(yvar[j])
> >       }
> >
> >       ## For auxiliary parameters:
> >       ##    1. Draw from base measure
> >       ##    2. Compute log probability for being in new cluster
> >       model$simulate(yparmsClust)
> >       for ( k in 1:naux ) {
> >         ## Temporarily change cluster membership
> >         model[[target]][j] <- k
> >
> >         ## Compute log probability for this cluster
> >         logProbs_mj_aux[k]  <- logProbNew_mj + model$calculate(yvar[j])  ## add on log likelihood
> >       }
> >
> >       ## Draw new cluster membership
> >       logProbs <- c(logProbs_mj_cl, logProbs_mj_aux)
> >       logProbs <- logProbs - logsumexp_vec(logProbs)
> >       znew_j   <- rcat( n = 1, prob = exp(logProbs) )
> >
> >       ## If znew refers to an auxiliary draw...
> >       if ( znew_j > max_components ) {
> >         ## If no empty clusters, throw error
> >         if ( length(clustEmpty_mj) == 0 )
> >           stop("Need to specify more maximum components")
> >         ## Otherwise, place in first empty cluster
> >         znew_j <- clustEmpty_mj[1]
> >
> >         ## HELP: need to store new value of parameter for this index; restore values for other clusters
> >
> >       }
> >       model[[target]][j] <<- znew_j
> >     }
> >
> >     ## Add new cluster membership to target
> >     model$calculate(target)
> >     model$calculate(yparmsClust)
> >     nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = target, logProb = TRUE)
> >     nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = yparmsClust, logProb = TRUE)
> >   }
> >   , methods = list(
> >     reset = function () {
> >       printMessage <<- TRUE
> >     }
> >   )
> > )
> >
> >

messages.subject: Equivalence of parameterisation for MCMC
messages.subject_clean: Equivalence of parameterisation for MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm generally interested in playing around with different parameterisations to improve MCMC mixing. I've got a high dimensional model that isn't mixing all that well. Specifically, it's an ordered probit item response model with correlated random individual and correlated random item effects on mu and sigma, with correlated random thresholds as well. So there's three seperate multivariate distributions in this model. I know the non-centered multivariate parameterisation is different from centered. However, I'd like to know, are the following two formulations equivalent in terms of MCMC sampling?

# Random individual effects for each individual i, ..., N
for (i in 1:n) {
   eps[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = eps.sigma)
   mu[i] <- alpha + eps[i]
   y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
}

vs.

for (i in 1:n) {
   mu[i] ~ dnorm(alpha, sd = eps.sigma)
   y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
}

I'd like to know because if these two formulations are the same, that simplifies the trial and error to see which approach mixes best. For instance, I've found that the centered multivariate thresholds mixes way better than the non-centered, but the non-centered multivariate item effects mix better than the centered. (FYI, I'm aware that the two formulations above aren't centered vs. non-centered but just two ways of writing the centered form.)

Thanks for reading!

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matthijs,
I suppose there is a prior on the alpha ?
If that is the case (as I suppose), then in terms of sampling both formulation are slightly different.
In the top one, each sampling of alpha triggers the update of all mu[i], and the evaluation of a density ratio (not sure of the statistical term for that) of all y[i] (as all mu[i] were modified)
In the bottom one, each sampling of alpha triggers the evaluation of all density ratio mu[i].

Given that, I think the top one would be slower but alpha would mix better, while the bottom one would be faster but alpha mixing would be worse.
If dimension is really high the top one should be too slow compared to the bottom one, but that is just a guess.

(This is just based on my knowledge on MCMC sampling though, I have no experience with this kind of model)
Hope this helps (and good luck !)
Rémi
