messages.body_snippet: Is it possible or are there plans to allow the user to pull the saved samples out of CModelMCMC and just keep the last sample along with mcmc parameters at that step (e.g., jump probabilities, etc.)?

messages.subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.subject_clean: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.body_plain:
Quresh, I think we have this functionality pretty well built-in, although I'm not sure how well documented this is... if it's documented at all.

Try:

## build and compile model and MCMC
mcmc$run(iterations)
samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
## save samples to disk
mcmc$run(more_iterations, reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE)   ## resets the internal mvSamples object, but leaves everything else the same
more_samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)

On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:56 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> Is it possible or are there plans to allow the user to pull the saved samples out of CModelMCMC and just keep the last sample along with mcmc parameters at that step (e.g., jump probabilities, etc.)? The idea would be to save the samples to the hard drive and keep on sampling without relying on RAM to store sampled iterations. This is what the `saveJAGS` package allows for JAGS, but JAGS is clearly a lot slower, so I'm wondering if there's any way to do this with NIMBLE.
>
> On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:44:41 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > Great, glad it helps.
> >
> > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:38 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > Ah, perfect! Thanks for pointing that out. I also see that you can set thinning when actually configuring the MCMC using the 'thin' argument (e.g., configureMCMC(Rmodel, thin = 10)). I don't see an argument for setting burn-in, but maybe I'm missing it? In any case, the option for setting thinning in the primary sampler is going to help a lot. Thank you!
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:24:59 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > Quresh, just set the thinning interval in the MCMC configuration object (using conf$setThin(INTERVAL), I believe), doing that before you build and compile the MCMC.  Then, even using mcmc$run(ITERATIONS) will respect the thinning interval, and only record those samples internally.
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:17 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > > One trade-off I am discovering with the above code is that because it uses the base function 'CModelMCMC$run' to allow resumption of sampling after checking convergence, I can't thin the samples as I go. I can thin after recovering the samples to save hard drive space, but the primary sampler does not allow thinning (or burn-in), which means that I end up running out of RAM before I reach convergence. For the time being, it seems like this code is useful at the initial stage of exploring a model, but once I have a sense of how long I'm going to need to run the sampler to get to convergence, I am probably going to have to switch to using the higher level 'nimbleMCMC' function, so that I can implement burn-in and thinning for better memory management.
> > > > >
> > > > > It might be nice for future versions of NIMBLE if either thinning/burn-in could be included in the base function (...$run) or if an option for resuming sampling could be incorporated into higher level functions that also allow thinning and burn-in.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Monday, August 15, 2022 at 11:23:43 AM UTC-6 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > >     }
> > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > >     })
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
> > > > > >     mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > >     #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     ## If has not converged, continue sampling
> > > > > >     n.reruns <- 0
> > > > > >     while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
> > > > > >       out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > >         CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > >         return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > >       })
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
> > > > > >       print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
> > > > > >       if(n.reruns == 1) {
> > > > > >         nb2 <- nb + nb
> > > > > >         ni2 <- ni + ni
> > > > > >       } else {
> > > > > >         nb2 <- nb2 + nb
> > > > > >         ni2 <- ni2 + ni
> > > > > >       }
> > > > > >       out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > >       out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > >       out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
> > > > > >       sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > >       sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > >         as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > >         mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > >         select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > >       #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > >       mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > >       gc(verbose = F)
> > > > > >     }
> > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday, January 20, 2022 at 2:57:06 PM UTC-7 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > hi Dan,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks for commenting here.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I've checked the example and I do get reproducible results using the code provided. I'm wondering if you modified it such that you are creating random initial values? If so, you'd need to use set.seed before you generate the initial values within the run_MCMC_allcode function.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > One other note is that the approach in that example relies on simply setting different seeds for the different chains. While this is probably safe, it is possible that the random numbers generated for one chain could partially overlap the random numbers generated for another chain. Even if this happened, I don't think it would cause substantive dependence between the chains. But your approach of using clusterSetRNGStream has the nice feature of ensuring the sequences of random numbers for each of the worker processes won't overlap.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > -chris
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Tue, Jan 18, 2022 at 11:36 AM Daniel Eacker <taurusw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > A bit late to add this, but I just wanted to add that I don't think this is correct for setting the seed in parallel processing using the parallel package:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > 1) In the `parLapply` call, the values of `X` are the values used for
> > > > > > > > the `seed` function. So it is used.

> > > > > > > > What I've found that works for repeatable results using parallel processing is to add this just after making the cluster:

> > > > > > > > e.g.,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > this_cluster <- makeCluster(2)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > clusterSetRNGStream(cl = this_cluster, 500) # note that 500 could be any integer.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > So, I don't think the X in parLapply actually does anything to produce repeatable results, whereas using this builtin function of the parallel package provides reproducible results.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Dan
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Thursday, April 2, 2020 at 11:39:15 AM UTC-8 db...@williams.edu wrote:

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 3) Towards that end - being able to start a new R session, and resume executing an MCMC chain precisely where it left off - I wrote a vignette about "Saving Model and MCMC State", which demonstrates how to save the model and MCMC state after executing an MCMC algorithm.  This is only demonstrated for a single chain, but could be generalized for the multi-chain case.  See the vignette here:

> > > > > > > > > Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Oh wow! Another game changer. I searched for 'resetMV' in the NIMBLE user manual and came up with nothing, so it's not documented in there. I'm not sure how to access the help file (or if there is one) for the ...$run function. In any case, I'll write some code that saves the samples to disk and post it here. Thanks so much!

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 12:27:17 PM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> Quresh, I think we have this functionality pretty well built-in, although I'm not sure how well documented this is... if it's documented at all.
>
> Try:
>
> ## build and compile model and MCMC
> mcmc$run(iterations)
> samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
> ## save samples to disk
> mcmc$run(more_iterations, reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE)   ## resets the internal mvSamples object, but leaves everything else the same
> more_samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
>
>
>
>
> On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:56 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > Is it possible or are there plans to allow the user to pull the saved samples out of CModelMCMC and just keep the last sample along with mcmc parameters at that step (e.g., jump probabilities, etc.)? The idea would be to save the samples to the hard drive and keep on sampling without relying on RAM to store sampled iterations. This is what the `saveJAGS` package allows for JAGS, but JAGS is clearly a lot slower, so I'm wondering if there's any way to do this with NIMBLE.
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:44:41 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > Great, glad it helps.
> > >
> > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:38 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > Ah, perfect! Thanks for pointing that out. I also see that you can set thinning when actually configuring the MCMC using the 'thin' argument (e.g., configureMCMC(Rmodel, thin = 10)). I don't see an argument for setting burn-in, but maybe I'm missing it? In any case, the option for setting thinning in the primary sampler is going to help a lot. Thank you!
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:24:59 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > > Quresh, just set the thinning interval in the MCMC configuration object (using conf$setThin(INTERVAL), I believe), doing that before you build and compile the MCMC.  Then, even using mcmc$run(ITERATIONS) will respect the thinning interval, and only record those samples internally.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:17 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > > > One trade-off I am discovering with the above code is that because it uses the base function 'CModelMCMC$run' to allow resumption of sampling after checking convergence, I can't thin the samples as I go. I can thin after recovering the samples to save hard drive space, but the primary sampler does not allow thinning (or burn-in), which means that I end up running out of RAM before I reach convergence. For the time being, it seems like this code is useful at the initial stage of exploring a model, but once I have a sense of how long I'm going to need to run the sampler to get to convergence, I am probably going to have to switch to using the higher level 'nimbleMCMC' function, so that I can implement burn-in and thinning for better memory management.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It might be nice for future versions of NIMBLE if either thinning/burn-in could be included in the base function (...$run) or if an option for resuming sampling could be incorporated into higher level functions that also allow thinning and burn-in.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Monday, August 15, 2022 at 11:23:43 AM UTC-6 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
> > > > > > >     mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > >     #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >     ## If has not converged, continue sampling
> > > > > > >     n.reruns <- 0
> > > > > > >     while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
> > > > > > >       out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > >         CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > >         return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > >       })
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >       n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
> > > > > > >       print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
> > > > > > >       if(n.reruns == 1) {
> > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb + nb
> > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni + ni
> > > > > > >       } else {
> > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb2 + nb
> > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni2 + ni
> > > > > > >       }
> > > > > > >       out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > >       out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > >       out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >       mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
> > > > > > >       sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > >       sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > >         as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > >         mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > >         select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > >       #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > >       mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > >       gc(verbose = F)
> > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday, January 20, 2022 at 2:57:06 PM UTC-7 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > hi Dan,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks for commenting here.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I've checked the example and I do get reproducible results using the code provided. I'm wondering if you modified it such that you are creating random initial values? If so, you'd need to use set.seed before you generate the initial values within the run_MCMC_allcode function.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > One other note is that the approach in that example relies on simply setting different seeds for the different chains. While this is probably safe, it is possible that the random numbers generated for one chain could partially overlap the random numbers generated for another chain. Even if this happened, I don't think it would cause substantive dependence between the chains. But your approach of using clusterSetRNGStream has the nice feature of ensuring the sequences of random numbers for each of the worker processes won't overlap.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > -chris
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Tue, Jan 18, 2022 at 11:36 AM Daniel Eacker <taurusw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > A bit late to add this, but I just wanted to add that I don't think this is correct for setting the seed in parallel processing using the parallel package:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1) In the `parLapply` call, the values of `X` are the values used for
> > > > > > > > > the `seed` function. So it is used.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I've tried this and it produces different results across MCMC simulations.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What I've found that works for repeatable results using parallel processing is to add this just after making the cluster:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > e.g.,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > this_cluster <- makeCluster(2)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > clusterSetRNGStream(cl = this_cluster, 500) # note that 500 could be any integer.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So, I don't think the X in parLapply actually does anything to produce repeatable results, whereas using this builtin function of the parallel package provides reproducible results.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Dan
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Thursday, April 2, 2020 at 11:39:15 AM UTC-8 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > To add just a few things:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 1) I'm not sure if there's any way to have the progress bar printed from one cluster node.  I agree, that would be nice.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 2) Even if you return the compiled object(s) from one cluster (looping over clusterExport(), as was suggested), these compiled objects still could not be saved (to be reloaded subsequently into a new R session) due to the current nature of NIMBLE's compilation and the resulting objects.  As I believe was mentioned, addressing this is a long-term goal for NIMBLE.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 3) Towards that end - being able to start a new R session, and resume executing an MCMC chain precisely where it left off - I wrote a vignette about "Saving Model and MCMC State", which demonstrates how to save the model and MCMC state after executing an MCMC algorithm.  This is only demonstrated for a single chain, but could be generalized for the multi-chain case.  See the vignette here:
> > > > > > > > > > https://danielturek.github.io/public/saveMCMCstate/saveMCMCstate.html
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Hope this helps!
> > > > > > > > > > Daniel
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Wed, Apr 1, 2020 at 12:56 PM Adrian Monroe <apm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Hi Ollie,
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Your connection to the clusters will be lost if you shut down R. That said, unless I am missing something, I don't see why you couldn't use clusterEvalQ() to return the necessary nimble objects from each cluster (such as in a list), save these nimble objects, then export the nimble objects back to individual clusters in another R session (looping clusterExport() through each cluster) and continue updating with more iterations. I am curious to see if that works, so please let me know how it goes.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I don't know about a progress bar, and the run times for each chain can be different so I don't know what one would really tell you.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > > > Adrian
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Sun, Mar 29, 2020 at 6:55 AM orwearn <oliver...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hi Adrian (and all),
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks for updating your code example. I have a follow-up query on it:
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Am I right in thinking that R cannot be closed between the initial run and the update in your code, because it depends on the same cluster ('cl') being open?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Is there a way of saving, exiting and then updating with more iterations at a later time (as possible in runjags etc.)? (I am running NIMBLE on Google Cloud, wherein it's difficult for me to keep R open for 3+ weeks...).
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Many thanks for any pointers from anyone, I'm only just starting to transition over from JAGS
> > > > > > > > > > > > Ollie
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > PS If there's a way to add a progress bar (e.g. just for node 1), that would also be a dream...! But not to worry if that isn't possible.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > On Sunday, March 29, 2020 at 1:14:01 AM UTC+7, Adrian Monroe wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Hi Ollie,
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > You bring up a good point, and I am sharing this with the rest of the nimble group to clarify. It seems indeed according to chapter 7 of the nimble help (https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html#sec:runMCMC) that runMCMC does NOT continue an MCMC run where it left off previously. I must have missed that, and I have modified the code for sampling and updating in parallel is below. Note the update returns all iterations from the start, not just the additional samples. Interestingly, when I used runMCMC to update, it didn't look to me like it was completely starting over, but instead was sampling from distributions it had reached previously (which is probably why I assumed it picked up from the previous run). If any of the nimble developers have some insights on this, and why reset = FALSE is not the default, I would be interested.
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Adrian
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > > > > > >   library(nimble)

messages.body_snippet: Oh wow! Another game changer. I searched for 'resetMV' in the NIMBLE user manual and came up with nothing, so it's not documented in there. I'm not sure how to access the help file (or if there is one

messages.subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.subject_clean: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.body_plain:
You're welcome!  It makes me happy to hear "another game changer".

It looks like it's only documented using help(buildMCMC) --- at least it's documented somewhere, I suppose.

Take a look for yourself, but I'll copy that documentation here:

     ‘resetMV’: Boolean specifying whether to begin recording posterior
     sample chains anew. This argument is only considered when using
     ‘reset = FALSE’.  Specifying ‘reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE’
     allows the MCMC algorithm to continue running from where it left
     off, but without appending the new posterior samples to the
     already existing samples, i.e. all previously obtained samples
     will be erased. This option can help reduce memory usage during
     burn-in (default = FALSE).

On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 2:37 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> Oh wow! Another game changer. I searched for 'resetMV' in the NIMBLE user manual and came up with nothing, so it's not documented in there. I'm not sure how to access the help file (or if there is one) for the ...$run function. In any case, I'll write some code that saves the samples to disk and post it here. Thanks so much!
>
> On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 12:27:17 PM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > Quresh, I think we have this functionality pretty well built-in, although I'm not sure how well documented this is... if it's documented at all.
> >
> > Try:
> >
> > ## build and compile model and MCMC
> > mcmc$run(iterations)
> > samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
> > ## save samples to disk
> > mcmc$run(more_iterations, reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE)   ## resets the internal mvSamples object, but leaves everything else the same
> > more_samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:56 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > Is it possible or are there plans to allow the user to pull the saved samples out of CModelMCMC and just keep the last sample along with mcmc parameters at that step (e.g., jump probabilities, etc.)? The idea would be to save the samples to the hard drive and keep on sampling without relying on RAM to store sampled iterations. This is what the `saveJAGS` package allows for JAGS, but JAGS is clearly a lot slower, so I'm wondering if there's any way to do this with NIMBLE.
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:44:41 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > Great, glad it helps.
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:38 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > > Ah, perfect! Thanks for pointing that out. I also see that you can set thinning when actually configuring the MCMC using the 'thin' argument (e.g., configureMCMC(Rmodel, thin = 10)). I don't see an argument for setting burn-in, but maybe I'm missing it? In any case, the option for setting thinning in the primary sampler is going to help a lot. Thank you!
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:24:59 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > > > Quresh, just set the thinning interval in the MCMC configuration object (using conf$setThin(INTERVAL), I believe), doing that before you build and compile the MCMC.  Then, even using mcmc$run(ITERATIONS) will respect the thinning interval, and only record those samples internally.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:17 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > > > > One trade-off I am discovering with the above code is that because it uses the base function 'CModelMCMC$run' to allow resumption of sampling after checking convergence, I can't thin the samples as I go. I can thin after recovering the samples to save hard drive space, but the primary sampler does not allow thinning (or burn-in), which means that I end up running out of RAM before I reach convergence. For the time being, it seems like this code is useful at the initial stage of exploring a model, but once I have a sense of how long I'm going to need to run the sampler to get to convergence, I am probably going to have to switch to using the higher level 'nimbleMCMC' function, so that I can implement burn-in and thinning for better memory management.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > It might be nice for future versions of NIMBLE if either thinning/burn-in could be included in the base function (...$run) or if an option for resuming sampling could be incorporated into higher level functions that also allow thinning and burn-in.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Monday, August 15, 2022 at 11:23:43 AM UTC-6 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
> > > > > > > >     mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > >     #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     ## If has not converged, continue sampling
> > > > > > > >     n.reruns <- 0
> > > > > > > >     while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
> > > > > > > >       out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > >         CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > >         return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > >       })
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
> > > > > > > >       print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
> > > > > > > >       if(n.reruns == 1) {
> > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb + nb
> > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni + ni
> > > > > > > >       } else {
> > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb2 + nb
> > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni2 + ni
> > > > > > > >       }
> > > > > > > >       out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >       out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >       out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
> > > > > > > >       sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > >       sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > >         as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > >         mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > >         select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > >       #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > >       mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > >       gc(verbose = F)
> > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Thursday, January 20, 2022 at 2:57:06 PM UTC-7 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > > hi Dan,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thanks for commenting here.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I've checked the example and I do get reproducible results using the code provided. I'm wondering if you modified it such that you are creating random initial values? If so, you'd need to use set.seed before you generate the initial values within the run_MCMC_allcode function.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > One other note is that the approach in that example relies on simply setting different seeds for the different chains. While this is probably safe, it is possible that the random numbers generated for one chain could partially overlap the random numbers generated for another chain. Even if this happened, I don't think it would cause substantive dependence between the chains. But your approach of using clusterSetRNGStream has the nice feature of ensuring the sequences of random numbers for each of the worker processes won't overlap.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > -chris
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Tue, Jan 18, 2022 at 11:36 AM Daniel Eacker <taurusw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > A bit late to add this, but I just wanted to add that I don't think this is correct for setting the seed in parallel processing using the parallel package:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 1) In the `parLapply` call, the values of `X` are the values used for
> > > > > > > > > > the `seed` function. So it is used.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I've tried this and it produces different results across MCMC simulations.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > What I've found that works for repeatable results using parallel processing is to add this just after making the cluster:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > e.g.,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > this_cluster <- makeCluster(2)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > clusterSetRNGStream(cl = this_cluster, 500) # note that 500 could be any integer.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > So, I don't think the X in parLapply actually does anything to produce repeatable results, whereas using this builtin function of the parallel package provides reproducible results.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Cheers,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Dan
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Thursday, April 2, 2020 at 11:39:15 AM UTC-8 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > To add just a few things:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > 1) I'm not sure if there's any way to have the progress bar printed from one cluster node.  I agree, that would be nice.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > 2) Even if you return the compiled object(s) from one cluster (looping over clusterExport(), as was suggested), these compiled objects still could not be saved (to be reloaded subsequently into a new R session) due to the current nature of NIMBLE's compilation and the resulting objects.  As I believe was mentioned, addressing this is a long-term goal for NIMBLE.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > 3) Towards that end - being able to start a new R session, and resume executing an MCMC chain precisely where it left off - I wrote a vignette about "Saving Model and MCMC State", which demonstrates how to save the model and MCMC state after executing an MCMC algorithm.  This is only demonstrated for a single chain, but could be generalized for the multi-chain case.  See the vignette here:

Subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model

You're welcome!  It makes me happy to hear "another game changer".

It looks like it's only documented using help(buildMCMC) --- at least it's documented somewhere, I suppose.

Take a look for yourself, but I'll copy that documentation here:

     ‘resetMV’: Boolean specifying whether to begin recording posterior
     sample chains anew. This argument is only considered when using
     ‘reset = FALSE’.  Specifying ‘reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE’
     allows the MCMC algorithm to continue running from where it left
     off, but without appending the new posterior samples to the
     already existing samples, i.e. all previously obtained samples
     will be erased. This option can help reduce memory usage during
     burn-in (default = FALSE).

On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 2:37 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> Oh wow! Another game changer. I searched for 'resetMV' in the NIMBLE user manual and came up with nothing, so it's not documented in there. I'm not sure how to access the help file (or if there is one) for the ...$run function. In any case, I'll write some code that saves the samples to disk and post it here. Thanks so much!

> On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 12:27:17 PM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:

> > Quresh, I think we have this functionality pretty well built-in, although I'm not sure how well documented this is... if it's documented at all.
> >
> >
> >
> > Try:
> >
> >
> >
> > ## build and compile model and MCMC
> >
> > mcmc$run(iterations)
> >
> > samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
> >
> > ## save samples to disk
> >
> > mcmc$run(more_iterations, reset = FALSE, resetMV = TRUE)   ## resets the internal mvSamples object, but leaves everything else the same
> >
> > more_samples <- as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples)
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:56 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> > > Is it possible or are there plans to allow the user to pull the saved samples out of CModelMCMC and just keep the last sample along with mcmc parameters at that step (e.g., jump probabilities, etc.)? The idea would be to save the samples to the hard drive and keep on sampling without relying on RAM to store sampled iterations. This is what the `saveJAGS` package allows for JAGS, but JAGS is clearly a lot slower, so I'm wondering if there's any way to do this with NIMBLE.

> > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:44:41 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:

> > > > Great, glad it helps.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:38 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> > > > > Ah, perfect! Thanks for pointing that out. I also see that you can set thinning when actually configuring the MCMC using the 'thin' argument (e.g., configureMCMC(Rmodel, thin = 10)). I don't see an argument for setting burn-in, but maybe I'm missing it? In any case, the option for setting thinning in the primary sampler is going to help a lot. Thank you!

> > > > > On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 10:24:59 AM UTC-6 db...@williams.edu wrote:

> > > > > > Quresh, just set the thinning interval in the MCMC configuration object (using conf$setThin(INTERVAL), I believe), doing that before you build and compile the MCMC.  Then, even using mcmc$run(ITERATIONS) will respect the thinning interval, and only record those samples internally.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Tue, Aug 23, 2022 at 12:17 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> > > > > > > One trade-off I am discovering with the above code is that because it uses the base function 'CModelMCMC$run' to allow resumption of sampling after checking convergence, I can't thin the samples as I go. I can thin after recovering the samples to save hard drive space, but the primary sampler does not allow thinning (or burn-in), which means that I end up running out of RAM before I reach convergence. For the time being, it seems like this code is useful at the initial stage of exploring a model, but once I have a sense of how long I'm going to need to run the sampler to get to convergence, I am probably going to have to switch to using the higher level 'nimbleMCMC' function, so that I can implement burn-in and thinning for better memory management.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > It might be nice for future versions of NIMBLE if either thinning/burn-in could be included in the base function (...$run) or if an option for resuming sampling could be incorporated into higher level functions that also allow thinning and burn-in.

> > > > > > > On Monday, August 15, 2022 at 11:23:43 AM UTC-6 Quresh Latif wrote:

> > > > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matthijs,

As you more or less have worked through by computational experiment, the mixing does differ, and it is problem-specific.  Here is a paper on that point: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/jcgs.2011.203main.

It has been an idea to implement a strategy like this automatically in nimble, although it would take some careful model inspection and processing of relationships.  If you or anyone is interested, please say so!

HTH!
Perry

On Thu, Aug 18, 2022 at 3:08 AM Rémi Patin <remi....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Matthijs,
> I suppose there is a prior on the alpha ?
> If that is the case (as I suppose), then in terms of sampling both formulation are slightly different.
> In the top one, each sampling of alpha triggers the update of all mu[i], and the evaluation of a density ratio (not sure of the statistical term for that) of all y[i] (as all mu[i] were modified)
> In the bottom one, each sampling of alpha triggers the evaluation of all density ratio mu[i].
>
> Given that, I think the top one would be slower but alpha would mix better, while the bottom one would be faster but alpha mixing would be worse.
> If dimension is really high the top one should be too slow compared to the bottom one, but that is just a guess.
>
> (This is just based on my knowledge on MCMC sampling though, I have no experience with this kind of model)
> Hope this helps (and good luck !)
> Rémi
>
>
> On 18/08/2022 10:09, Matthijs Hollanders wrote:
> > Whoops... the sigma[i] above should just be sigma.
> >
> > On Thursday, August 18, 2022 at 6:08:10 PM UTC+10 Matthijs Hollanders wrote:
> > > Hello all,
> > >
> > > I'm generally interested in playing around with different parameterisations to improve MCMC mixing. I've got a high dimensional model that isn't mixing all that well. Specifically, it's an ordered probit item response model with correlated random individual and correlated random item effects on mu and sigma, with correlated random thresholds as well. So there's three seperate multivariate distributions in this model. I know the non-centered multivariate parameterisation is different from centered. However, I'd like to know, are the following two formulations equivalent in terms of MCMC sampling?
> > >
> > > # Random individual effects for each individual i, ..., N
> > > for (i in 1:n) {
> > >    eps[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = eps.sigma)
> > >    mu[i] <- alpha + eps[i]
> > >    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
> > > }
> > >
> > > vs.
> > >
> > > for (i in 1:n) {
> > >    mu[i] ~ dnorm(alpha, sd = eps.sigma)
> > >    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
> > > }
> > >
> > > I'd like to know because if these two formulations are the same, that simplifies the trial and error to see which approach mixes best. For instance, I've found that the centered multivariate thresholds mixes way better than the non-centered, but the non-centered multivariate item effects mix better than the centered. (FYI, I'm aware that the two formulations above aren't centered vs. non-centered but just two ways of writing the centered form.)
> > >
> > > Thanks for reading!
> > >
> > > Matt

Hi again everyone,
I am working on turning my R functions to nimble and I have one that wraps several other functions returns a list and returns a list of the output of these. I looked at the details of returnType in chapter 11 of the nimble users manual and it doesnt look like a list is a possible output, is this correct? If not, I should be able to work around it by just calling the four functions themselves rather than the wrapper.
Thanks
Ben

On Monday, August 22, 2022 at 5:20:51 PM UTC-6 Ben Padilla wrote:
>
> Hi Perry,
>
>
>
> Thanks a lot for taking a stab at it despite my somewhat unclear questions. After thinking through things a bit more, I realize that there is really just one function I want to call within the nimblecode. I’ve also just finally just come to recognize why the nimble functions, or nimbleRcall are necessary – the R code needs to be compiled into the C language in order to work with the MCMC sampler. Sorry I’m a bit slow on that, I often forget all of the work arounds that are required to get an MCMC sampler working within R.
>
>
>
> The one thing I’d like to incorporate into my nimble model is the `bigmatrix` function (code below), everything else just needs to be loaded in to the R environment prior to analysis. This bigmatrix function is a wrapper for the four demographic functions that define the population projections, so these functions would all need to be either written as nimbleFunctions, or translated to a nimbleFunction via nimbleRcall, as would the bigmatrix function itself.
>
>
>
> I must admit I am not entirely up to speed on all the clever ways nimble models can be worked with and adapted. While I’ve used nimble for several projects I’ve always simply called the model code through nimbleMCMC rather than through the more adaptable multi-step process. That said, I want the inputs and outputs of this function to interact with different nodes of the model I already have, so I don’t know if it would be possible to call the model from within the nimbleRcall. Though, my understanding of all the details there is admittedly limited.
>
>
>
> Thanks,
>
> Ben
>
>
>
> #################################################################
>
> # FUNCTION TO CONSTRUCT COMPONENTS OF THE IPM KERNAL
>
> ################################################################
>
>
>
> bigmatrix<-function(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params) {
>
>   S <- Surv.fun(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params["surv_int"],
>
>                   bigmatrix.params["surv_slope"], bigmatrix.params["starvation_ratio"],
>
>                   bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_surv"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])
>
>
>
>   R <- Repro.fun(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params["zs_threshold_k"], bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],
>
>                   bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"],
>
>                    bigmatrix.params["steepness"], bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"],
>
>                    bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"], bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"],bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"],
>
>                    bigmatrix.params["breeding_zr_threshold"], bigmatrix.params["neonate_mortality"], params["Veg_max"], params["mean_warbles"],
>
>                    bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_fecund"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"], bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])
>
>
>
>   G <- G.fun(zr_50, zs_50,bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"],bigmatrix.params["steepness"],bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],
>
>              bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"],bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"], bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"],
>
>              bigmatrix.params["zs_threshold_k"], bigmatrix.params["breeding_zr_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ReproZ"], bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ZS"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_1"],
>
>              bigmatrix.params["Veg_max"],bigmatrix.params["mean_warbles"],bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"],bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])
>
>
>
>   D <- D.fun (zr_50, zs_50, bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],  bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"], bigmatrix.params["steepness"],bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],
>
>               bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"],bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"],bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"],
>
>               bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"], bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"], bigmatrix.params["ReproZ_to_OffspringZS"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_2"],
>
>               bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ReproZ"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_3"], bigmatrix.params["Veg_max"],
>
>               bigmatrix.params["mean_warbles"],bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"], bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])
>
>
>
>   return(list(S=S,R=R,G=G,D=D))
>
> }
>
>
>
> --
>
> Benjamin Padilla Ph.D
> Postdoctoral Research Associate
>
> University of Calgary
>
> Twitter: @bpdilla
>
> Web: www.benpadilla.weebly.com <http://www.benpadilla.weebly.com>
>
>
>
>
>
> From: Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu>
> Date: Monday, August 22, 2022 at 1:27 PM
> To: Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com>
> Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: Calling external script from within nimble model?
>
> Hi Ben,
>
>
>
> I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.
>
>
>
> First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
>
>
>
> What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
>
>
>
> myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
>
>   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
>
>   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
>
>   # etc.
>
> }
>
>
>
> my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
>
>
>
> m <- nimbleModel(...)
>
> cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
>
>
>
> If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
>
>
>
> Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?
>
>
>
> HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?
>
>
>
> Perry
>
>
>
>
>
> On Mon, Aug 22, 2022 at 11:44 AM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello All,
> >
> >
> >
> > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> >
> >
> >
> > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> >
> >
> >
> > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> >
> >
> >
> > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> >
> >
> >
> > for(i in 1:nYears){
> >
> > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> >
> > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> >
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> >
> > for(i in 1:nndat){
> >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> >   }
> >
> >
> >
> > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> >
> >
> >
> > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.
> >
> >
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > Ben
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

nimbleCode({
...
S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])
...
})

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

Perry

Hi Perry,

Thanks for your time as always!

Ah, of course, a nimbleList! I think that given my objectives keeping my four demographic functions separate makes the most sense. To give a bit of background, the inputs of all of these are either vectors or single numeric values, and the outputs are vectors for survival (S) and reproduction (R) and are matrices for the growth and development functions (G and D). I then want to use these to estimate a population vector within the model using matrix algebra, similar to this:

PopVector  <- G %*% (S * PopVector[t-1]) + D %*% (R* PopVector[t-1])

The ‘bigmatrix.params’ is a numeric list of parameters that go into the S,R,G and D functions. So, yes, you are right this would be in the R environment, or supplied to the model as data. Ideally I would be able to change iteratively within the model presumably using some indexing (though I am not sure if this will work in the nimble context).

I think I am getting there but there is still a ways to go. Looking at the code for the one example of the type of model I’m trying to build, which happens to have been written in nimble, is also helping me along.  Thanks for the help!

Hi Ben,

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

Perry

> > >   }

messages.subject: Beta-binomial N-mix with p-rho parameterization
messages.subject_clean: Beta-binomial N-mix with p-rho parameterization
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm interested in using the beta-binomial observation model for an N-mixture model, as described in this linked paper <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00113.x>, but I would like to implement the p-rho parameterization rather than the alpha-beta that they implement.

Briefly, here's how they accomplish the BBP N-mix:

# Observation model for replicated counts

for (i in 1:n) {​ # Loops over all n observations

C[i] ~ dbin(p[i], N[site.p[i]]) # counts follow a beta-binomial distribution

       p[i]~dbeta(alpha.p,beta.p)  # detection probability p follows a beta distribution

}
The p-rho would be where p is the probability parameter and rho is a correlation parameter. I would rather use the p-rho because currently I have covariates on p. I think this is the version that the dNmixture_BBP_*() functions use, which is great, but then I'm not sure how to carry out PPC/GOF tests when using the nimbleEcology distributions.

Might anyone be able to pass along example code for the p-rho beta-binomial, or instead example code for a PPC/GOF test using dNmixture_BBP_*()?

Sincere thanks!

Best,
Gates Dupont

messages.subject: dNmixture_*() use with missing counts
messages.subject_clean: dNmixture_*() use with missing counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I would love to use the dNmixture_*() distributions. I'm analyzing "citizen science" data, though, so I have around 700 sites with up to 9 surveys, but some of those sites completed only as few as 4 surveys.

Is there a straightforward way of handling this sort of missing data using the dNmixture_*() distributions? Passing the data as a 700 x 9 matrix (that I call "C") with missing counts as NAs does not seem to work automatically.

I know I have to loop through sites and provide all surveys to dNmixture_s() as C[i,1:nsurveys], which is the complicating factor because will be NAs in there. I have some ideas that might get around this (e.g., dynamic indexing perhaps), but nothing straightforward given the irregular data. I just want to make sure there isn't something on the nimble side of things to facilitate this, like an `na.rm = T` option.

Thank you,
Gates

hi Ethan,

To restore all parameter values when a subject belongs to an existing cluster, you could do something like this:

nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = clusterParamsToRestore, logProb = TRUE)

where clusterParamsToRestore is a vector of node names (I think this is yparmsClust in your case.)

To revert the parameters for all but the new cluster, you could exclude the new cluster from the clusterParamsToRestore.

nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = clusterParamsToRestore[-idx], logProb = TRUE)

However, I'm not sure if "-idx" will work in compiled code, so you might need to do something like:

nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = clusterParamsToRestore[1:(idx-1)], logProb = TRUE)
nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = clusterParamsToRestore[(idx+1):P], logProb = TRUE)

and you'd need to protect against cases where idx = 1 or idx = P.

Actually, it might be easier to revert for all of them via nimCopy (including overwriting the one you want to update) and then only for the new cluster, assign the new value back into the model via
model[[nodeName]] <<- ...
or
values(model, nodeNames) <<- ...

Of course you'd need to have saved the updated value in a temporary variable before it got overwritten in the model by the nimCopy.

Let me know if I'm not quite on target with what you need or you have further questions.

-chris

> > > > >
> > > > > #' Compute log V_n(t) as in Miller and Harrison
> > > > > #'
> > > > > #' @param t number of partitions
> > > > > #' @param n sample size
> > > > > #' @param lambda mean hyperparameter for poisson prior on k-1
> > > > > #' @param gamma dirichlet parameter
> > > > > #' @param tol tolerance for sum
> > > > > #' @return computation of log V_n(t)
> > > > > logvn <- nimbleFunction(
> > > > >   run = function(
> > > > >       t      = integer(0)
> > > > >     , n      = integer(0)
> > > > >     , lambda = double(0)
> > > > >     , gamma  = double(0)
> > > > >     , tol    = double(0, default = 1e-12)
> > > > >   ) {
> > > > >     returnType(double(0))
> > > > >     thresh <- 1.0 - tol     ## the sum decays faster than the poisson CDF
> > > > >     ## Number of partitions t must be <= n
> > > > >     if ( t > n )
> > > > >       return(-Inf)
> > > > >     a <- 0.0      ## Previous value of log V_n(t)
> > > > >     c <- -Inf     ## Computation of log V_n(t)
> > > > >     k <- 1        ## counter for the sum
> > > > >     p <- 0.0      ## poisson CDF calculation (to be compared with thresh)
> > > > >     while ( abs(a-c) > tol | p < thresh ) {
> > > > >       if ( k >= t ) {
> > > > >         gamma_k <- gamma * k
> > > > >         a       <- c
> > > > >         b       <- lgamma(k+1) - lgamma(k-t+1) - lgamma(gamma_k + n) + lgamma(gamma_k) + dpois(k-1, lambda, 1)
> > > > >         c       <- logsumexp(a, b)
> > > > >       }
> > > > >       p <- p + dpois(k-1, lambda, 0)
> > > > >       k <- k + 1
> > > > >     }
> > > > >     return(c)
> > > > >   }
> > > > > )
> > > > >

> > > > > #'

> > > > > #'
> > > > > #' @return a vector giving sizes of clusters whose elements are 1:max_components
> > > > > getClusterSizes <- nimbleFunction(
> > > > >   run = function(x = double(1), max_components = integer(0)) {
> > > > >     returnType(double(1))

> > > > > #' \itemize{

> > > > > #'    \item "empty" a vector of cluster indexes that are empty
> > > > > #' }
> > > > > getClusterIndexes <- nimbleFunction(
> > > > >   run = function(x = double(1)) {

> > > > >     returnType(membershipList())
> > > > >     max_components <- length(x)

> > > > >   }
> > > > > )

> > > > >

> > > > > #' Computes the mass function for the modified CRP of Miller
> > > > > #'
> > > > > #' @param x vector giving cluster membership
> > > > > #' @param size length of x
> > > > > #' @param lambda parameter for poisson prior on (number of components - 1)
> > > > > #' @param gamma parameter for Dirichlet prior on membership probability
> > > > > #' @param tol tolerance for computing log normalizing constant
> > > > > #' @param log whether to return on log scale
> > > > > #'
> > > > > #' @return a scalar giving the mass function for the cluster membership
> > > > > dMCRP <- nimbleFunction(
> > > > >   run = function(
> > > > >       x = double(1)
> > > > >     , size = integer()
> > > > >     , lambda = double(0)
> > > > >     , gamma = double(0)

> > > > >   contains = sampler_BASE,
> > > > >   setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {

> > > > >   }
> > > > >   , run = function() {

> > > > >
> > > > >     ## Create copy of cluster-specific parameters

> > > > >
> > > > >     for ( j in 1:n ) {

messages.body_plain:
Hi all. I modified the code above to include all of the desired functionality noted in previous posts (parallel processing, resuming after checking convergence, thinning the primary sampler in each cluster, saving to the hard drive to avoid overloading RAM). The code appears to be working well in the script I have running for my particular project, but when I try to put the code in an R function (see attached), I am getting an error on line 17 ("Error in get(name, envir = envir) : object 'init' not found"). Not sure if this is a fixable problem, or if this is just not a task that works from within a function. Any insight would be appreciated. In the meantime, perhaps the code contained within the attached (not yet operational) function will prove useful to folks here.

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
> > > > > > > > >     mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > > >     #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     ## If has not converged, continue sampling
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >     n.reruns <- 0
> > > > > > > > >     while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
> > > > > > > > >       out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > >         CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > > >         return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > > >       })
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
> > > > > > > > >       print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
> > > > > > > > >       if(n.reruns == 1) {
> > > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb + nb
> > > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni + ni
> > > > > > > > >       } else {
> > > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb2 + nb
> > > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni2 + ni
> > > > > > > > >       }
> > > > > > > > >       out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > >       out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > >       out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >       mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
> > > > > > > > >       sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > >       sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > > >         as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > > >         mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > > >         select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > > >       #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > > >       mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > > >       gc(verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > >     }
