Hi again folks,

I am back with yet another question. Thanks to your guidance and the great resources you and others have made available online I managed to get some nimbleFunctions written up and worked into my model. For a first step I decided not to estimate the integral projection model functions within the model, so the parameterization cannot be dynamic, but the body size distribution of the population can easily be calculated based on the current distribution and the getPopVec function.

The code passes successfully through nimbleModel(), but when I try to compile it I get the following error. I searched through the code in detail trying to see anything that is not properly indexed but cant find the issue.

cIPM2 <- compileNimble(IPM2_mod)

Compiling

  [Note] This may take a minute.

  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.

confused about trying to eigenize something with nDim = 0

Called from: sizeAssignAfterRecursing(code, symTab, typeEnv)

Browse[1]> c

Error in if (RHSnDim > 0) { : argument is of length zero

I’ve attached the model code in its entirety, but the only portion that is changed from the state-space population model that this is built off of is below.

  # Estimate projection matrix with the IPM_ind

  #############################################

  for(yr in 2:nYear){

    PopVector[1:nmass,yr] <- getPopVec(S[1:nmass],R[1:nmass],G[1:nmass,1:nmass],D[1:nmass,1:nmass],PopVector[1:nmass,yr-1],2)

  }

Thanks in advance!

--

Benjamin Padilla Ph.D
Postdoctoral Research Associate

University of Calgary

Twitter: @bpdilla

Web: www.benpadilla.weebly.com <http://www.benpadilla.weebly.com>

> > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > >
> > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > >
> > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > >
> > >   # etc.
> > >
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > >
> > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?
> > >
> > >

> > >

> > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > >
> > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > >
> > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > >
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > >
> > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks,
> > > >
> > > > Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

I just looked in the documentation for clusterExport and it indicates that the default location where variables (such as 'init') are looked for is in the global environment:

  ‘clusterExport’ assigns the values on the master R process of the
     variables named in ‘varlist’ to variables of the same names in the
     global environment (aka ‘workspace’) of each node.  The
     environment on the master from which variables are exported
     defaults to the global environment.

So it looks like you'll have to modify the `envir` argument to tell clusterExport to look in the local environment of the function call to find init.

Or you could just export all the inits to all the workers and then on the worker side determine which element of the inits to use.

-Chris

> > > > > > > > > > Hello all. I realize this is an older post, but thought I'd share that I was able to successfully build on Adrian's code. The code below implements parallel processing, checks Rhats for specified parameters, and if they are too low, it keeps resuming until Rhats meet the desired threshold. The calculation of Rhats leverages the 'mcmcOutput' package. Perhaps others may find this useful.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#
> > > > > > > > > >     library(parallel)
> > > > > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> > > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))
> > > > > > > > > >     mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > > > >     #sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% arrange(desc(Rhat)) %>% View()
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     ## If has not converged, continue sampling
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >     n.reruns <- 0
> > > > > > > > > >     while(round(mxRht, digits = 1) > 1.1) {
> > > > > > > > > >       out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > > >         CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > > > >         return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > > > >       })
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       n.reruns <- n.reruns + 1
> > > > > > > > > >       print(str_c("Reruns = ", n.reruns))
> > > > > > > > > >       if(n.reruns == 1) {
> > > > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb + nb
> > > > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni + ni
> > > > > > > > > >       } else {
> > > > > > > > > >         nb2 <- nb2 + nb
> > > > > > > > > >         ni2 <- ni2 + ni
> > > > > > > > > >       }
> > > > > > > > > >       out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > >       out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb2+2, ni2+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > >       out.mcmc.update <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >       mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc.update)
> > > > > > > > > >       sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > > >       sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > > > >         as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > > > >         mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > > > >         select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > > > >       #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > > > >       mxRht <- sumTab %>% slice(ind.Rht) %>% pull(Rhat) %>% max(na.rm = T)
> > > > > > > > > >       gc(verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > > >     }

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you use the lowest-level entry point to NIMBLE's MCMC engine, the run() method of the compiled MCMC object, then at that level there's the ability to "continue" an on-going run using reset=FALSE. messages.body_plain:
Perry or Henry,

I know this thread is a year old now, but do either of you have a very simple code example demonstrating this system2() + Rscript approach for repeatedly building and compiling nimble models when the data structure and model constants are changing from one simulation to the next?

Thanks,
Glenn

On Tuesday, August 10, 2021 at 6:16:14 PM UTC-5 henryr...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Perry,
>
> Thanks for the quick reply and helpful suggestions. I think the system2() + Rscript workout will work for me. The memory use during some preliminary runs using system2() looked good.
> Not having to rebuild and compile is tempting, but the data structures for the various simulation scenarios are pretty intricate and I'm reluctant to kick that nest.
>
> Best,
> Henry
>
> On Monday, August 9, 2021 at 6:02:51 PM UTC-7 pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Henry,
> >
> > This is a tricky issue.  We have built two features to attempt to reduce memory use, but still it seems that objects evade R's garbage collection.  This may be because we have a lot of reference class objects and environments, creating potentially closed loops of referenced objects.  The two features are:
> >
> >   nimbleOptions(clearNimbleFunctionsAfterCompiling = TRUE) # This can modestly reduce memory use
> >
> >   nimble:::clearCompiled(model) # This attempts to clear all compiled content for the project related to model and to unload the on-the-fly compiled shared library used for it.
> >
> > However I tried both of these and they don't resolve the issue you're reporting.  It's something we'll have to look into more.   We have worked on this in the past but this doesn't look like good behavior.
> >
> > Here are some potential workarounds.
> >
> > You could within each loop use system2() to call Rscript and launch a self-contained process.  This would make sense if you really need to do the full nimble building and compilation each time.
> >
> > If you are really re-using the same model structure, you could build and compile just once and then simply re-assign data values.  e.g.
> > Cmodel$y <- some_other_values
> > then re-run your already-compiled MCMC.
> >

> >

> > >

> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >     #~~~~~~~~~Parallel processing code (won't work in Windows)~~~~~~~~~#

> > > > > > > > > > >     library(coda)
> > > > > > > > > > >     set.seed(3)
> > > > > > > > > > >     cl<-makeCluster(nc, timeout = 5184000)
> > > > > > > > > > >     clusterExport(cl, c("model", "inits", "data", "constants", "parameters", "ni"))
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >     for (j in seq_along(cl)) {
> > > > > > > > > > >       set.seed(j)
> > > > > > > > > > >       init <- inits()
> > > > > > > > > > >       clusterExport(cl[j], "init")
> > > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >     out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> > > > > > > > > > >       library(nimble)
> > > > > > > > > > >       library(coda)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >       model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >                            constants = constants, data = data,
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >                            inits = init)
> > > > > > > > > > >       Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > > > > > > > >       modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >       CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
> > > > > > > > > > >       return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > > > > > > > > > >     })
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >     ## Check convergence ##
> > > > > > > > > > >     out2 <- out1
> > > > > > > > > > >     out2[[1]] <- out2[[1]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > > >     out2[[2]] <- out2[[2]][seq(nb+2, ni+1, by = nt),]
> > > > > > > > > > >     out.mcmc <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out2, coda::as.mcmc))
> > > > > > > > > > >     #traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"])
> > > > > > > > > > >     library(mcmcOutput)
> > > > > > > > > > >     #if(nc > 1) mod.raw <- coda::as.mcmc.list(lapply(out$samples, coda::mcmc))
> > > > > > > > > > >     mod <- mcmcOutput(out.mcmc)
> > > > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- summary(mod, MCEpc = F, Rhat = T, n.eff = T, f = T, overlap0 = T, verbose = F)
> > > > > > > > > > >     sumTab <- sumTab %>%
> > > > > > > > > > >       as_tibble() %>%
> > > > > > > > > > >       mutate(Parameter = row.names(sumTab)) %>%
> > > > > > > > > > >       select(Parameter, mean:f)
> > > > > > > > > > >     #MCMCvis::MCMCtrace(out.mcmc, params = "DELTA1[114, 2]", pdf = F, ISB = F)
> > > > > > > > > > >     ind.Rht <- which(!str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "test.n") &
> > > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "M.save") &
> > > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "pXtheta") &
> > > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "Ind") &
> > > > > > > > > > >                        !str_detect(sumTab$Parameter, "ind"))

> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >

I am having this same problem and have tried so many things to no avail.. I reinstalled xcode, commandline tools, and R... where can i find the .R/Makevars file?

>

> > Hey Perry and Duncan,
> >
> > After reinstalling Xcode, commandline tools, and R, I just deleted my .R/Makevars and then it worked. Hopefully there aren't other consequences to doing that but I saved the Makevars I had before so probably all good.

> > >
> > > You might check the output of the  shell command-line call

> > >
> > > If the output doesn't say something like  /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools, but instead says ..../Developer, you probably need to set it, e.g.,
> > >
> > > sudo xcode-select -s /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools
> > > See SO <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57494601/clang-cant-compile-basic-header-files-like-iostream-in-macos> question.
> > >
> > > Worth a try.
> > > D.

> > > > Ann

messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura, Perry
 -c
Look to see if there is a directory ~/.R, i.e. $HOME/.R.   If it is there,see if contains a file named Makevars or Makevars-...  which may be for a platform-specific file.
It is an optional file one can use to override some of R's make configuration variable.
R uses this file (if it exists) and also the one in R_HOME/etc${R_ARCH}/Makeconf

These are places to explore what command line arguments are being given.

>From the error message, the command line seems to start with

clang++ -arch arm64 -std=gnu++14 -I"/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/include" -DNDEBUG -DR_NO_REMAP   -DEIGEN_MPL2_ONLY=1 -I"/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.2-arm64/Resources/library/nimble/include" -Wno-misleading-indentation -Wno-ignored-attributes -Wno-deprecated-declarations  -I/opt/R/arm64/include   -fPIC  -falign-functions=64 -Wall -g -O2  -c dynamicRegistrations_08_25_12_44_29.cpp -o

There is a bit after the -o that is truncated but probably not important.

Perhaps put the following code
#include <string>

int
foo(std::string x)
{
    return(x.size());
}

into a file named, say, str.cc and then give the shell command

clang++ -c str.cc

and see what errors come from that. You can share the whole output  with us.

Also, run the shell command
 R CMD config CXX
and see what the output for that is - hopefully  the same instance of clang++ as you are finding on your shel's own path.

D.

messages.body_plain:
Hi again Folks,
First off, I apologize for posting again here. I feel I am taking up a lot of valuable space here with what should be simple questions. I've been doing some more digging and thinking on what could be causing this error preventing the model to compile. It seems to have something to do with a random number generation error. In my R functions that I passed through nimbleRcall I have used the rnegbin() function in the MASS package to generate a per-individual parasite load. As I understand it this wont work within nimble. I looked at the  code underlying the rnegbin function to try and translate it to nimble, but it uses the rpois function, so that likely wont work even if I package it within a nimbleFunction. It occurs to me that someone may have a nimble version already coded?
Thanks
Ben

I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

> > > > Hi Ben,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > >
> > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > >
> > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > >
> > > >   # etc.
> > > >
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > >
> > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Perry
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, Aug 22, 2022 at 11:44 AM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hello All,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > >
> > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > >
> > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > >
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > >
> > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > >   }
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.

> > > > >

> > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

> > > > >
> > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

> > > > > }

> > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > >
> > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > >
> > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > >
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > >   }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Hi Ben,

Here's my process.

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.

Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.
I see pVec is created from
pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)
which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)
There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

You do also need a returnType statement.

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

Here is a modification that works:

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})
CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

Does that look like what you need?
Perry

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: Averaging models in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Averaging models in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hanah

I'll assume that you are fitting the models via MCMC, that the MCMC mixing is equally good for each model, and that you have the same number of samples (and similar effective sample sizes <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/coda/versions/0.19-4/topics/effectiveSize>) per model. Section 7.6 of the manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html#sec:extracting-samples> covers how to extract samples for a single model. You will simply need to extract your samples for each of your N models, combine those N matrices into a single matrix (e.g. using rbind) and perform all further analyses with this new matrix.  If memory becomes an issue due to matrix size (i.e. nrow becoming big) then simply define some thinning rule to reduce matrix size.

Hope that helps
David

Hi Ben,

Here's my process.

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

You do also need a returnType statement.

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

Here is a modification that works:

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Perry
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Mon, Aug 22, 2022 at 11:44 AM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hello All,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.

> > > > > > >

> > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > >

messages.subject_clean: what to do when you need to use a parameter value as an index?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working on an age-structured mark-recapture model with time- and age-specific survival and (re)capture rates. Right now, I am assuming age can be determined with certainty, so I am able to make age a data value, not a parameter. As a result, I can use age to access time- and age-specific rates--e.g. phi[t-1,age[i,t-1]]. However, there is substantial error in the ageing process, so I need to make age a parameter so I can account for its state uncertainty. Is there a workaround so I can use age as an index to call up age-specific rates even though age will now be a parameter?

Thank you!

Rebecca

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Thanks for responding so quickly. Let me try again. The problem is not how to make age a parameter. The problem is how to use a parameter as an index.

In particular, I need to be able to access a matrix of time- and age-specific rates using the parameter age[i,t].

For example, consider the 73rd individual in my data set  at time 2. In any given iteration, it will have an age of "age[73,2]", and it would survive with rate "phi[2, age[73,2]]". But Nimble doesn't seem to want me to use a parameter as an index for phi. As far as I can tell, I can only use a data value or a constant as an index.

Does that make sense?

Rebecca

> There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

>
>
> pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

>

>

>
>

> getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
>     returnType(double(1))
>     pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
>     if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
>     return(pVec)
> })

>
>

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

> > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > }

> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. Hi Ben,

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

HTH
Perry

> >

> >

> >
> >
> >
> > The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

> >     pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
> >     if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]

> > > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.

> Big picture -- you don't need to set up an MCMC for the predictive model. You just need to use `simulate` on the appropriate nodes in `ppSamplerNF`, including any y's that you want to sample from the predictive distribution.

If you don't set 'y' as data, then the whole thing is predictive and a posterior_predictive_branch sampler would be assigned to theta and would also include conditional sampling of y given the sampled value of theta.

Benjamin Padilla Ph.D
Postdoctoral Research Associate

University of Calgary

Twitter: @bpdilla

From: Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu>

Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: rnegbin equivalent in NIMBLE? / Calling external script from within nimble model

Hi Ben,

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

HTH

Perry

On Fri, Aug 26, 2022 at 4:44 PM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:

> >
> > There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:
> >
> >
> >
> > pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]
> >
> >
> >
> > where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.
> >
> >
> >
> > You do also need a returnType statement.
> >
> >
> >
> > The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.
> >
> >
> >
> > I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.
> >
> >
> >
> > Here is a modification that works:
> >
> >
> >
> > getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
> >     returnType(double(1))
> >     pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
> >     if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
> >     return(pVec)
> > })

> > > > > > However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > nimbleCode({
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ...
> > > > > >
> > > > > > S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ...
> > > > > >
> > > > > > })
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

> > > > > > > > Hi Ben,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Perry
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > On Mon, Aug 22, 2022 at 11:44 AM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hello All,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Ben

Good Morning Perry,

In my initial formulation of the getPopVec function I had specified seas2sim as a single value (double(0)) with the intent of using it in a for loop (ie, in 1:seas2sim), I hadn’t noticed that when you kindly re-wrote the function to be compatible with nimble you’d changed it to double(1). I simply changed the value in the model code from 2 to c(1,2) and the model compiled successfully. That was a silly bit of oversight on my part, sorry I didn’t catch it on my own!

Ben

Hi Ben,

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

HTH

Perry

> > > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

> > > > > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Ben

> I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.
>
>
>
> A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

> > > > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this, Adrian!

Follow-up question. Playing around with this today. It seems `dNmixture_s()` expects the observation data (here, C) to be in the form of, generally: C[site, first_count:last_count]

I'm trying to use `dNmixture_s()` for a multi-year multi-species model, though. So, for species `b` in year `t`, the right-hand side would look like:

dNmixture_s(
      lambda = lambda[t,b],
      prob = p[t,b],
      Nmin = 0, Nmax = 500,
      len = length_survey[n])

I don't know exactly what the left-hand side should look like. I tried C[b, first_count:last_count], but got the "multiple definitions for node(s)" error for all C[,] values.

Should I instead us C[site, first_count:last_count] and have nested species indexes for first_count:last_count that I would then use for `lambda` and `prob` too? Or something else?

I can share some reproducible code if it would help. Haven't yet found a multi-species or multi-year example for the dNmixture distributions, would love to see one if it's out there.

Thank you!
Gates

> >
> > Is there a straightforward way of handling this sort of missing data using the dNmixture_*() distributions? Passing the data as a 700 x 9 matrix (that I call "C") with missing counts as NAs does not seem to work automatically.
> >
> > I know I have to loop through sites and provide all surveys to dNmixture_s() as C[i,1:nsurveys], which is the complicating factor because will be NAs in there. I have some ideas that might get around this (e.g., dynamic indexing perhaps), but nothing straightforward given the irregular data. I just want to make sure there isn't something on the nimble side of things to facilitate this, like an `na.rm = T` option.
> >
> > Thank you,
