messages.body_plain:
Hey Gates,

I think the dNmix’s implement a closed model, so you could treat each year by site as a separate site with a distinct len—maybe defining some grouping variable if you wanted a site or site by species random effect.

John

> On Aug 29, 2022, at 1:51 PM, Gates Dupont <gd8...@princeton.edu> wrote:
>
> ﻿I meant to add: alternatively, might `dNmixture_s()` allow C to be a three-dimensional array? Such that: C[nsites, nsurveys, nspecies].

>
> Thanks!
> Gates
>
> On Monday, August 29, 2022 at 3:44:57 PM UTC-4 Gates Dupont wrote:
> > Thanks for this, Adrian!
> >
> > Follow-up question. Playing around with this today. It seems `dNmixture_s()` expects the observation data (here, C) to be in the form of, generally: C[site, first_count:last_count]
> >
> > I'm trying to use `dNmixture_s()` for a multi-year multi-species model, though. So, for species `b` in year `t`, the right-hand side would look like:
> >
> > dNmixture_s(
> >       lambda = lambda[t,b],
> >       prob = p[t,b],
> >       Nmin = 0, Nmax = 500,
> >       len = length_survey[n])
> >
> > I don't know exactly what the left-hand side should look like. I tried C[b, first_count:last_count], but got the "multiple definitions for node(s)" error for all C[,] values.
> >
> > Should I instead us C[site, first_count:last_count] and have nested species indexes for first_count:last_count that I would then use for `lambda` and `prob` too? Or something else?
> >
> > I can share some reproducible code if it would help. Haven't yet found a multi-species or multi-year example for the dNmixture distributions, would love to see one if it's out there.
> >
> > Thank you!
> > Gates
> > On Wednesday, August 24, 2022 at 5:20:47 PM UTC-4 apm...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hi Gates,
> > >
> > > You could try passing your observations as a vector rather than a matrix, removing the missing counts. Mason Fidino had a nice blog post on this: https://masonfidino.com/nested_indexing/
> > >
> > > Adrian
> > >
> > > On Wed, Aug 24, 2022 at 3:10 PM Gates Dupont <gd8...@princeton.edu> wrote:
> > > > Hi all,
> > > >
> > > > I would love to use the dNmixture_*() distributions. I'm analyzing "citizen science" data, though, so I have around 700 sites with up to 9 surveys, but some of those sites completed only as few as 4 surveys.
> > > >
> > > > Is there a straightforward way of handling this sort of missing data using the dNmixture_*() distributions? Passing the data as a 700 x 9 matrix (that I call "C") with missing counts as NAs does not seem to work automatically.
> > > >
> > > > I know I have to loop through sites and provide all surveys to dNmixture_s() as C[i,1:nsurveys], which is the complicating factor because will be NAs in there. I have some ideas that might get around this (e.g., dynamic indexing perhaps), but nothing straightforward given the irregular data. I just want to make sure there isn't something on the nimble side of things to facilitate this, like an `na.rm = T` option.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you,
> > > > Gates

Many thanks for this. Glad to hear dNmix should be able to handle additional indexing -- I'm working on a simulated example now to get a feel for it. My inferential objective is estimating overall expected abundance (lambda), and I'm not (yet) exploring site-level variation, so lambda and p aren't varying across sites. There are 16 species, 33 years, and over 700 sites, so the model already takes 4 days to run without including site-level effects, which is becoming a bit prohibitive. So that's why I don't think the indexing of lambda and p would be the issue -- maybe that makes sense?

Thanks again!
Gates

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much, David!

Best regards,
Hanah

On Friday, 26 August 2022 at 16:34:30 UTC+2 David Pleydell wrote:
> Hi Hanah
>
> I'll assume that you are fitting the models via MCMC, that the MCMC mixing is equally good for each model, and that you have the same number of samples (and similar effective sample sizes <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/coda/versions/0.19-4/topics/effectiveSize>) per model. Section 7.6 of the manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html#sec:extracting-samples> covers how to extract samples for a single model. You will simply need to extract your samples for each of your N models, combine those N matrices into a single matrix (e.g. using rbind) and perform all further analyses with this new matrix.  If memory becomes an issue due to matrix size (i.e. nrow becoming big) then simply define some thinning rule to reduce matrix size.
>
> Hope that helps
> David
>
>

messages.subject: Re: dNmixture_*() use with missing counts
messages.subject_clean: dNmixture_*() use with missing counts
messages.body_plain:
As an update... I've created a data object (C) as a 4D array with the structure: C[n_sites, n_visits, n_years, n_species], where NA values are moved to the tail of each row of C, which allows me to have another matrix for the length of each survey to feed to dNmix.

However, since not every site reports every year, I have some rows of C that are entirely NA, such that the survey length is then 0. That will not work with dNmix because 1:surv_length[i] will become 1:0 and that will give in error. Although there are over 200,000 observations, the amount of "missing data" under the 4D format is 90%, which is substantial.

Back to the drawing board! I think I will need to convert back to the nested indexing idea. Still open to any suggestions. Thank you!

Best,
Gates

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

I wanted to follow up with another thanks. After working through some issues with how I had the model coded (I was getting no posterior variance for the parameters estimated with the getPopVec function) I now have a working model. Now I just need to fully integrate the likelihoods of various components as well. This is all thanks to your help and much appreciated!

Ben

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   # etc.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > m <- nimbleModel(...)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.1364>). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020 <https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/708723>. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nYears){
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > for(i in 1:nndat){
> > > > > > > > > >     ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
> > > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me.

> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Perry. I have further clues that I'd like your advice on. Because this bug only occurred rarely and the code takes a long time to run, I set up a workflow that I thought would isolate the iteration the bug was occurring on and hopefully let me find it. Here is the workflow:

1. compile model, run some iterations, save model and mcmc states
2. in a for loop
2a. recompile model, load model and mcmc states, set seed, run 2500 iterations
2b. save model and mcmc states and loop iteration.
2c. repeat until crash
3. restart Rstudio, recompile model, load model and mcmc states, set the same seed used for the loop iteration of the crash, run until the iteration of the crash
4. Inspect mcmc states, look for something that might cause the bug, perhaps repeat above also printing sampler number to see where it crashes

I got to step 3, but nimble didn't crash on the same iteration. I thought I must have messed up the workflow. I tested it and I confirmed I was restarting correctly and it should work. I gave up and just ran it again.

This time, it crashed while building the model, not while running or even compiling!  Looking at a screen shot at the link below, you see it completed the 2500 iterations and printed "defining model". I see no other interpretation than it crashed while building the model.

https://twitter.com/BenCAugustine/status/1564988783480766468/photo/1

Does this suggest to you the problem is not nimble? Perhaps Rstudio is crashing at random with respect to what nimble is doing? Any insight would be useful.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gates--

Indexing is definitely a hassle as models get bigger, so I totally understand the headache.

Thanks for sending along reproducible code. I was able to diagnose the "multiple definitions" error. You're looping over nsurveys and using dynamic indexing to extract observations for each species based on a start and end vector. All of the model code looks fine. The issue appears to be that "start_obs" and "end_obs" contain duplicates, such that as you loop through surveys, you're going back over your start/end. For example, survey 1 is associated with obs 1-4, but survey 42 is associated with obs 1-5. Maybe you're trying to have different values for each species? In that case, you could make start_obs and end_obs matrices.

Hope this helps. In general, I always find dynamic indexing easiest if the data are as "long form" as possible, with columns I can use to dynamically index parameters, groups, etc. You seem to be going down that track.

Ben

On Tue, Aug 30, 2022 at 1:51 PM Gates Dupont <gd8...@princeton.edu> wrote:

> As an update... I've created a data object (C) as a 4D array with the structure: C[n_sites, n_visits, n_years, n_species], where NA values are moved to the tail of each row of C, which allows me to have another matrix for the length of each survey to feed to dNmix.
>
> However, since not every site reports every year, I have some rows of C that are entirely NA, such that the survey length is then 0. That will not work with dNmix because 1:surv_length[i] will become 1:0 and that will give in error. Although there are over 200,000 observations, the amount of "missing data" under the 4D format is 90%, which is substantial.
>
> Back to the drawing board! I think I will need to convert back to the nested indexing idea. Still open to any suggestions. Thank you!
>
> Best,
> Gates

There are 16 species, 33 years, and over 700 sites, so the model already takes 4 days to run without including site-level effects, which is becoming a bit prohibitive.
